notes.b:
• Pure substance: melts/boils at a sharp temperature; impurities lower m.p. and raise b.p.
  • Chromatography: Rf = distance moved by component ÷ distance moved by solvent front.
  • Choose separation by property: filtration (insoluble solid), crystallization (heat-sensitive soluble solid), simple/fractional distillation (by b.p.), separating funnel (immiscible liquids).
  • Titration: rinse burette with solution to be filled, pipette with solution it measures; indicator = methyl orange/phenolphthalein.

• n = m/M; concentration c = n/V (mol/dm³); gas volume n = V/24 dm³ at r.t.p.
  • Empirical formula: % ÷ Ar → divide by smallest → whole-number ratio.
  • % yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
  • Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons (e.g. ¹²C, ¹⁴C).

• Ionic: metal + non-metal; giant lattice; conducts when molten/aqueous; high m.p.
  • Covalent: non-metals sharing; simple molecular = low m.p., non-conductor (except graphite); giant covalent (diamond, SiO₂) = very hard, high m.p.
  • Metallic: ions in sea of delocalised electrons → conducts, malleable.
  • Dot-and-cross diagrams expected for NaCl, MgO, H₂O, CO₂, CH₄.

• OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.
  • Electrolytes: molten/aqueous ionic compounds or acids. Inert electrodes (Pt/graphite) vs active electrodes (Cu).
  • Brine (conc. NaCl): cathode H₂, anode Cl₂, solution becomes NaOH.
  • Electroplating & copper refining use active Cu anode that dissolves.
  • Half-equation example: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation at anode).

• Exothermic: combustion, neutralisation, respiration (ΔH negative). Endothermic: thermal decomposition, photosynthesis, dissolving NH₄Cl.
  • Energy profile diagrams with activation energy labelled.
  • Collision theory: rate ↑ with concentration, temperature, surface area, catalyst (lowers Eₐ).
  • Read rate graphs: gradient = rate; curve flattening = reactant used up; comparing curves at same time.

• Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂; acid + metal → salt + H₂; acid + alkali → salt + water (neutralisation).
  • pH scale; universal indicator colours; strong vs weak acids.
  • Soluble salt prep: titration for Na/K/NH₄⁺ salts; excess insoluble reactant + filter + crystallize for others.
  • Insoluble salt prep: precipitation, e.g. AgCl, BaSO₄ — mix two soluble salts, filter, wash, dry.

• Group I: soft, reactive (↑ down), float, H₂ + alkali. Group VII: coloured, less reactive down; halogen displacement (Cl₂ displaces Br₂, I₂).
  • Transition metals: high m.p., variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, catalysts (Fe, Ni, Pt).
  • Reactivity series: K Na Ca Mg Al Zn Fe Pb Cu Ag — determines displacement & extraction method.
  • Blast furnace: haematite + coke + limestone → iron + slag (CaSiO₃).

• Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (saturated, burn, substitution with Cl₂); alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (test: decolourise bromine water; addition; hydration → ethanol); alcohols R–OH (fermentation of glucose, oxidation → acid); carboxylic acids R–COOH (weak acids, esters with alcohols).
  • Isomerism from butane/C₄H₁₀ onwards.
  • Homologous series = same general formula, similar properties, gradual trends, differ by CH₂.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come (Paper 2): Section of structured questions — define/state (1–2 marks, one line each), explain using structure/bonding (3–4 marks, always link property → particle behaviour), write symbol/half equations, and calculations (moles, titration, yield) where working must be shown — error carried forward applies. Paper 6 gives drawn apparatus (burette readings, gas syringe) and asks you to describe the experiment, complete tables, and conclude. Command words: State, Define, Explain, Describe, Suggest, Calculate, Plan.

flash.a: Relights a glowing splint.
Burning splint → 'pop' sound.
Bubble through limewater → turns milky (white precipitate of CaCO₃).
Bleaches damp litmus paper (white).
Turns damp RED litmus paper BLUE; white fumes with HCl.
Family of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, successive members differ by CH₂.

flash.q: Products of electrolysis of concentrated NaCl (brine)?
flash.a: Cathode: hydrogen. Anode: chlorine. Solution left: sodium hydroxide.

flash.q: Why does increasing temperature increase rate of reaction?
flash.a: Particles have more kinetic energy → collide more often AND with greater energy exceeding activation energy → more successful collisions per second.

solved.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ NaOH is exactly neutralised by 22.40 cm³ of HCl. Find the concentration of the HCl. [3]
steps: Equation: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂ — mole ratio 1:1.
Moles HCl = same = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol (1:1 ratio).
solved.a: Answer: 0.167 mol/dm³ (3 s.f.). Full marks need the 4 written steps.

solved.q: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O. Find its empirical formula. [3]
steps: Divide by smallest (3.33): C = 1, H = 2, O = 1.
Ratio 1 : 2 : 1.
solved.a: Empirical formula = CH₂O (this is also the molecular formula of glucose if M = 180 ÷ 30 = 6 × CH₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆).

solved.t: Why H₂ not Na at the cathode in brine?
solved.q: During electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution with inert electrodes, hydrogen (not sodium) forms at the cathode. Explain. [3]
steps: Both Na⁺ and H⁺ (from water) are attracted to the cathode.
H⁺ is much lower than Na⁺ in the reactivity series — discharged more easily.
Each H⁺ gains an electron: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
solved.a: Hydrogen is lower in the reactivity series, so its ions are preferentially discharged.

practice.q: 1. Calculate the mass of 0.25 mol of CaCO₃. (Aᵣ: Ca 40, C 12, O 16) [2]
2. Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. [2]
practice.a: Graphite has delocalised electrons between its layers that are free to move and carry charge; in diamond every electron is held in strong covalent bonds — no free electrons or ions.

practice.q: 3. A student compares the rate of reaction of magnesium ribbon vs magnesium powder with excess acid. State and explain two expected differences. [3]
practice.a: Powder reacts faster: (1) greater surface area → more particles exposed → more frequent successful collisions; (2) both produce the same final volume of hydrogen (same moles of Mg) but powder finishes sooner — curve steeper, levels at same height.

practice.q: 4. Describe how to prepare a pure, dry sample of the insoluble salt lead(II) sulfate. [4]
practice.a: Mix solutions of lead(II) nitrate and sodium sulfate (both soluble) → white PbSO₄ precipitates. Filter, wash residue with distilled water to remove soluble impurities, dry between filter papers / in low oven.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.tag: UPDATED SYLLABUS (exams 2024–2026): Paper 1 is now READING, Paper 2 is now WRITING — 2 hours each.

papers.d: Section A (25): comprehension of a narrative text (~900 words) — explicit + implicit meanings, language analysis. Section B (25): summary writing (max 150 words) + short response on implicit meanings/attitudes. No dictionaries.

Section A (25): Directed Writing — ONE compulsory task based on stimulus text(s); respond in 250–350 words, discursive/argumentative/persuasive. Section B (25): Composition — ONE from four titles (2 descriptive, 2 narrative), 350–450 words.

notes.b:
• Answer in your OWN words unless told to quote.
  • 1 mark = 1 distinct point. 2 marks = two separate points, not one point explained.
  • Inference formula: 'This suggests that ___ because the text says ___' — always anchor with a short quotation.
  • Language questions: identify technique (imagery, contrast, alliteration, rhetorical question) → quote → effect on reader.

• Read the task's focus line FIRST — only lift points answering it.
  • Aim for 12–15 brief points in rough, then combine into ONE paragraph of ≤150 words.
  • Change the grammar (noun→verb etc.) to prove own-words; no examples, no repetition, no opinions.
  • Use connectives: furthermore, consequently, in addition, however.

notes.t: 3. Directed Writing (P2 Section A) — the game changer
notes.b:
• Underline the 3 stimulus facts you MUST use — marks are awarded for using them.
  • Decide register from audience: formal (principal, official) vs informal (friend).
  • Structure: intro stating purpose → 2–3 developed paragraphs (Point → stimulus evidence → effect) → short conclusion with recommendation.
  • Write 250–350 words; five focused paragraphs beat ten thin ones.

notes.t: 4. FORMAT BANK — Directed Writing genres (P2 Section A, 250–350 words)
notes.b:
The task always names a genre — its features carry marks:
  • Speech: greet the audience (“Good morning, teachers and friends”); rhetorical questions, direct address (“you”), repetition for emphasis; end with a memorable call to action + “Thank you”.
  • Formal letter: sender's address top right → date → recipient's address left; “Dear Sir/Madam” pairs with “Yours faithfully”, “Dear Mr/Ms + name” with “Yours sincerely”; formal paragraphs, no contractions.
  • Email: To/Subject header optional; greeting + short paragraphs matched to the named audience (formal to the principal, relaxed to a friend); clear sign-off.
  • Report: title + To/From/Date/Subject header; subheaded sections; impersonal tone (“It was found that…”); finish with recommendations.
  • Article: headline (+ optional byline); engaging opening, semi-formal lively style, one idea per paragraph, strong conclusion.
Always: weave in the 3 required stimulus points, hold the stated audience/purpose in every line, and stay inside 250–350 words — content past 350 is not credited.

• Descriptive: 5-senses detail, strong verbs, pathetic fallacy, vary sentence openings ('Despite the rain…'), build atmosphere before event.
  • Narrative: hook in line 1 (action/dialogue/short shock sentence), clear climax, end with resolution or echo of the opening.
  • Show don't tell: 'His knuckles whitened around the letter' not 'He was nervous'.

• Formal: no contractions, no slang, complete sentences, respectful tone.
  • Informal: contractions, exclamations, direct address, conversational idioms.
  • Sentence variety examiners love: one short punch ('Silence.') between two complex sentences.
  • Plan for 5 minutes before writing — a plan converts a C answer into an A answer.

• Read 15–20 minutes daily (quality news, features, short stories): underline unknown words, guess meaning from context first, then check — this builds the exact skill inference questions test.
  • Skim and scan drills: gist in 60 seconds (title + first/last line of each paragraph); scanning — find a name, date or number in a text as fast as possible.
  • Own-words drill: take one sentence from a text and rewrite it three different ways (synonyms, grammar changes) — comprehension marks depend on this.
  • Inference formula: “This suggests that … because the text says …” — always anchor an interpretation with a short quotation.
  • Mark-scheme study: after every past-paper attempt, read the mark scheme to learn how short, precise answers are phrased — 1 mark = 1 distinct point, never one point explained twice.
  • Summary cutting drill: reduce a 300-word passage to the word limit — delete examples, repetition, descriptions and figures of speech; keep only points that answer the focus line.

• Plan 3–5 minutes every time: bullet the task points, order them, decide the register (formal/informal) BEFORE writing — unplanned writing rambles and misses bullets.
  • Memorise one flexible skeleton per genre (see the FORMAT notes above) until you can reproduce it automatically — in the exam you spend your energy on ideas, not structure.
  • Weekly timed practice: one full task in exact exam time, then self-mark with a checklist: all bullets covered? register consistent? paragraphs linked? word count inside the limit?
  • Upgrade vocabulary deliberately: 5 new collocations per week in a notebook, and force them into your next practice piece (e.g. “a worthwhile experience”, “raise awareness”).
  • Vary sentence openings: fronted adverbials (“Surprisingly,…”, “Despite this,…”), mix short punchy sentences with longer complex ones — examiners reward controlled variety.
  • Keep an accuracy pass: reserve the last 3–4 minutes to check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, capital letters and end punctuation.
  • Rewrite, don't just re-read: get one piece marked each week and rewrite the SAME piece improved — rewriting is where the marks actually grow.

notes.t: 9. Good to know — assessment is 100% written
notes.b:
1123 has NO speaking and NO listening component — your entire grade comes from Paper 1 (Reading) and Paper 2 (Writing). Unlike IGCSE ESL (0510) there is no speaking endorsement. Put all speaking-practice time into vocabulary and reading instead — it pays off directly in both papers.

  • Reading feeds writing: note down 2–3 strong phrases from every Paper 1 text you practise and reuse them in your compositions.
  • The summary (Section B) is the most trainable 25 marks in the whole syllabus — drill one summary per week against the mark scheme.

subjects.fmt: New format highlights (2024–2026): Papers swapped names — Paper 1 is now Reading, Paper 2 is Writing, both 2 hours. The Reading paper now rewards writing skills (clear own-words answers, structured summary) and the Writing paper rewards reading skills (using the stimulus). Composition word count is 350–450 words and Directed Writing response is 250–350 words. Attempt Section B of P2 with a title you can VISUALISE — description of a place/scene is statistically the friendliest choice.

flash.a: Only points answering the focus line, in your own words, ONE paragraph, ≤150 words, connected with linking words. Never add your own opinion.
This suggests that… because the text says '…' (quote). Claim + evidence = full marks.
Correct format · audience-appropriate register · at least 3 stimulus facts woven in · developed paragraphs · clear conclusion/recommendation.
Formal: no contractions (do not), full forms, polite modal verbs. Informal: contractions, exclamations, direct address, idioms.
In medias res action, dialogue, rhetorical question, short shocking sentence, sensory snapshot.
5 minutes minimum. Plan converts a C answer into an A answer.

solved.q: Focus line: 'Summarise the problems the writer faced during the mountain trek.' The passage contains 18 points; 9 relate to the focus. [15]
steps: Underline every sentence about PROBLEMS ONLY: weather, altitude sickness, lost trail, low food, injured porter, equipment failure, night cold, thin air, fear.
Convert each to own words: 'weather' → 'severe storms slowed progress daily'.
Drop: scenery descriptions, solutions, opinions, examples.
Combine overlapping points (storms + cold → 'harsh weather conditions').
Write one paragraph ~140 words, 7–9 points, connectives between them.
solved.a: Examiners award ~2 marks per 2 correct own-words points; adding non-focus content LOSES marks.

solved.t: Directed Writing model plan (P2 Q1 style)
solved.q: Stimulus: school canteen survey — long queues, unhealthy food, high prices, students skipping lunch. Task: write a report/proposal to the principal suggesting improvements. [25]
steps: Format: report — title, To/From, introduction, findings with the 4 survey facts, recommendations (3: staggered breaks, healthier menu with pricing, pre-order system).
Register: formal. Use: 'It is recommended that…', 'The survey reveals that…'.
Develop each recommendation: what + why it fixes a stated problem + expected benefit.
Conclusion: polite call to action, willingness to help implement.
solved.a: A Band-5 answer names all 4 stimulus problems, proposes a linked solution for each, and keeps the formal report structure.

practice.q: 1. Write ONE inference about a character who 'folded the map for the seventh time, eyes scanning every path except the one home.' [2]
practice.a: Own-words inference: he is avoiding returning home (1) — evidence: deliberately ignores the route home / repeated folding shows agitation (1).

practice.q: 2. List the 5 features of a formal speech.
practice.a: Direct address to audience, rhetorical questions, rule of three, emotive vocabulary, formal register with clear opening and closing thanks.

practice.q: 3. Plan (intro + 3 paragraph topics + conclusion) a descriptive composition: 'The marketplace at dawn.'
practice.a: Intro: sensory snapshot (sound/smell/light). P1: stalls awakening — colours, vendors. P2: the crowd builds — movement, noise, haggling. P3: a focal scene — one vendor and customer. Conclusion: dawn fully broken, day beginning — echo opening image.

practice.q: 4. In the summary, why is copying phrases from the passage penalised?
practice.a: Summary tests selection AND re-expression; copied phrases show no language skill — 1 mark per point is lost if wording is lifted.

subjects.tag: Untiered (no Core/Extended) — everyone sits the same papers. 0990 is the identical 9–1 graded version.

papers.d: Q1(a–e) comprehension of Text A (15). Q1(f) summary of Text B, max 120 words (15). Q2 language task — analyse 3 examples from 2 paragraphs, 200–300 words (20). Q3 extended response to Text C in a given format — letter/report/journal/speech/interview/article, 250–350 words (30).
Section A: Directed Writing from text stimulus (40). Section B: Composition — choose 1 of 4 (descriptive/narrative titles) (40).
Portfolio route in place of Paper 2 at some schools.
Separate endorsement, does not affect grade.

notes.b:
• Texts on ONE theme come in an insert; read all three before starting.
  • Q1(a–e): short comprehension — own words, 1 mark per point.
  • Q1(f): summary ≤120 words of Text B for the given focus.
  • Q2: the LANGUAGE question — pick 3 striking word/phrase choices per paragraph, quote, name technique, explain effect.
  • Q3: uses Text C ideas in a required format — the format's features earn marks (headline, salutation, sign-off...).

• Quote + technique + meaning + effect on reader. E.g. 'the word "devoured" (violent verb / personification) suggests the sea consumed the coast greedily, making the destruction feel alive and terrifying'.
  • Never list techniques without linking to effect — that caps you at half marks.

• ≤120 words, own words, one paragraph, focus-line only points, connectives.
  • Cross out your rough notes — examiners check you selected, not copied.

• Two texts give opposing views; you evaluate both and give a developed opinion.
  • Paragraph pattern: idea from text → your evaluation → developed example.
  • Both texts MUST be referred to for the top band.

notes.t: 5. FORMAT BANK — Extended-response genres (P1 Q3 / P2 Section A, 250–350 words)
notes.b:
The question names the genre — format features are marked:
  • Letter: addresses + date; correct salutation/sign-off pairing (Dear Sir/Madam → Yours faithfully; Dear Ms Khan → Yours sincerely).
  • Report: To/From/Subject/Date header, subheadings, objective tone, recommendations at the end.
  • Journal/diary: date at top; first person; informal reflective voice — thoughts and feelings, no address block.
  • Speech: greet the audience, rhetorical questions, direct address, strong closing line.
  • Interview: Q&A layout — Interviewer: question / Name: answer; realistic spoken register that still answers the task.
  • Article: headline, engaging hook, paragraph per point, voice matched to the named readership.
Rule: whatever the genre, sustain voice + audience + purpose from first line to last — that is where most of the marks live.

• Descriptive: zoom-in structure — wide shot, zoom to detail, one focal moment, wide again.
  • Narrative: controlled structure, tension curve, dialogue punctuation perfect.
  • Accurate complex sentences with subordinate clauses are the style band's currency.

• Read 15–20 minutes daily (quality news, features, short stories): underline unknown words, guess meaning from context first, then check — this builds the exact skill inference questions test.
  • Skim and scan drills: gist in 60 seconds (title + first/last line of each paragraph); scanning — find a name, date or number in a text as fast as possible.
  • Own-words drill: take one sentence from a text and rewrite it three different ways (synonyms, grammar changes) — comprehension marks depend on this.
  • Inference formula: “This suggests that … because the text says …” — always anchor an interpretation with a short quotation.
  • Mark-scheme study: after every past-paper attempt, read the mark scheme to learn how short, precise answers are phrased — 1 mark = 1 distinct point, never one point explained twice.
  • Summary cutting drill: reduce a 300-word passage to the word limit — delete examples, repetition, descriptions and figures of speech; keep only points that answer the focus line.

0500-specific: Q2 (language analysis) improves fastest by building a technique glossary — metaphor, personification, alliteration, contrast, rule of three, emotive diction — and drilling the formula quote → technique → meaning → effect on the reader for every text you read.

• Plan 3–5 minutes every time: bullet the task points, order them, decide the register (formal/informal) BEFORE writing — unplanned writing rambles and misses bullets.
  • Memorise one flexible skeleton per genre (see the FORMAT notes above) until you can reproduce it automatically — in the exam you spend your energy on ideas, not structure.
  • Weekly timed practice: one full task in exact exam time, then self-mark with a checklist: all bullets covered? register consistent? paragraphs linked? word count inside the limit?
  • Upgrade vocabulary deliberately: 5 new collocations per week in a notebook, and force them into your next practice piece (e.g. “a worthwhile experience”, “raise awareness”).
  • Vary sentence openings: fronted adverbials (“Surprisingly,…”, “Despite this,…”), mix short punchy sentences with longer complex ones — examiners reward controlled variety.
  • Keep an accuracy pass: reserve the last 3–4 minutes to check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, capital letters and end punctuation.
  • Rewrite, don't just re-read: get one piece marked each week and rewrite the SAME piece improved — rewriting is where the marks actually grow.

notes.t: 9. SKILL BUILDER — Speaking & Listening (Component 4 — optional endorsement)
notes.b:
How 0500 speaking works: Component 4 is optional and reported as a separate endorsement — it does not change your written grade. It is assessed as an individual talk plus discussion. If your school enters you, prepare like this:

  • Daily 5-minute self-talk: pick any topic card, speak aloud non-stop — structure every answer as opinion → reason → example → personal experience.
  • Record yourself on your phone; replay and hunt for long pauses, repeated fillers (“um, like”), and problem sounds (th, v/w, p/b). Re-record until clean.
  • Build a phrase bank: opinions (“In my view…”, “I'm convinced that…”), polite disagreement (“I see your point, but…”, “That's true to an extent, however…”), buying time (“Well, let me think…”).
  • Never give one-word answers — extend everything (Answer–Extend–Example). A short answer with development beats a perfect sentence that says nothing.
  • Shadowing: play a podcast/news clip and repeat each sentence aloud immediately — this fixes rhythm, stress and intonation faster than reading.
  • Exam day: don't memorise speeches (examiners spot them instantly); speak naturally — small mistakes are fine if communication stays clear and fluent.

subjects.fmt: Timing (Cambridge's own guide): Q1(a–e) 15–20 min · Q1(f) 20 min · Q2 35 min · Q3 40 min. Q3 is worth 30/80 — it is the single biggest question on the paper. Read the required format carefully: a journal needs dates and reflection; an interview needs Q&A turns; a report needs headings.

flash.a: Quote → identify technique → what it means → effect on the reader. Four steps, every time.
120 words maximum, one paragraph, own words.

flash.q: Q3 response length and what earns the format marks?
flash.a: 250–350 words. Format features: e.g. letter (address, salutation, sign-off), report (title, headings), speech (direct address, rhetorical questions).

flash.q: What must a top-band Directed Writing do?
flash.a: Refer to BOTH stimulus texts, evaluate their ideas, add own developed examples, and reach a clear personal judgement.

flash.q: Q2 language question: how many examples?
flash.a: Three relevant examples from EACH specified paragraph, quoted and analysed in continuous prose (200–300 words).

solved.q: 'The town clung to the cliff like a frightened child.' Analyse the writer's use of language. [3]
steps: Quote: 'clung... like a frightened child'.
Technique: simile + personification (verb 'clung').
Meaning: the town seems fragile, desperate, holding on for safety.
Effect: reader feels the town's vulnerability and the danger of the cliff — empathy and tension.
solved.a: All four steps in 2–3 sentences = 3/3. Technique named with no effect = max 1.

solved.q: Text B has 600 words; focus = 'advantages of city life'. [15]
steps: 3 min: read, underline only focus-relevant points (aim 12–14).
4 min: convert each to own words in rough.
8 min: write one flowing paragraph ≤120 words.
Never spend more than 20 min here — Q3 (30 marks) needs 40.
solved.a: One point ≈ one mark; own-words expression is essential; stay under 120 words.

practice.q: 1. What is the difference between a journal entry and a report as Q3 formats?
practice.a: Journal: dated entries, personal reflective tone, first person. Report: impersonal, headings, findings/recommendations, formal.

practice.q: 2. Give 3 features of an interview format.
practice.a: Alternating interviewer questions and interviewee answers, brief scene-setting intro, reported or scripted speech, balanced turn-taking.

practice.q: 3. Analyse: 'The silence was a thick blanket over the valley.' [3]
practice.a: Metaphor (silence = blanket) → silence feels heavy, smothering, total → creates stillness/unease; 'thick' intensifies the weight the reader senses.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.tag: Count-in Speaking route is most common: Core P1+P3+P5 or Extended P2+P4+P6. Syllabus is revised from 2027 — verify components for YOUR exam year before revising.

papers.d: Core = Paper 1; Extended = Paper 2 (higher difficulty, uncapped grades).
Heard twice; note-form answers common — spelling of key words still matters.
Interview + discussion on a topic card. 'Count-in Speaking' includes it in your grade; otherwise reported separately.

notes.b:
• Skim for gist (2 min), then read the questions BEFORE the detail scan — answers follow text order.
  • Exercises 1–4: MCQ, matching, note-completion and short answers. For note-completion copy NO MORE THAN 3 words unless told otherwise; spelling of copied words must be exact.
  • Never leave blanks — guess from context; wrong answers don't lose extra marks.

Skeleton:
  • Subject line: short and on-task (e.g. “My visit to your city”).
  • Greeting: Hi / Dear + first name → new paragraph.
  • Para 1: opening reference (“Thanks for your email — great to hear from you!”).
  • Paras 2–3: cover EVERY bullet point in the task, one idea per paragraph; informal register throughout — contractions (I'm, can't), phrasal verbs, direct questions (“Why don't you come too?”).
  • Para 4: closing line (“Write back soon!”, “See you there!”).
  • Sign-off: Best wishes / Take care / Love + your first name on the next line.
Marks go to: task fulfilment (all bullets answered), friendly tone held to the end, accurate everyday grammar. No addresses, no date, no “Dear Sir” — formal features cost marks here.

Skeleton (usually for a school magazine/website):
  • Title/headline: short and engaging — a question or strong phrase (“Is homework a waste of time?”).
  • Para 1: hook the reader + your main point (anecdote, question, surprising fact).
  • Paras 2–3: develop 2–3 task-bullet ideas with examples and opinion; lively semi-formal tone — direct address allowed (“Have you ever…?”).
  • Para 4: conclusion — final opinion or call to action.
Marks go to: covering the bullets, clear paragraphs, engaging style, linkers (however, moreover, on the other hand).

notes.t: 4. FORMAT — Report / Essay / Review (Exercise 6 options, 120–160 words)
notes.b:
• Report (e.g. to the headteacher): title + To/From/Subject header; subheaded sections (Introduction / Findings / Recommendations); factual, impersonal, no slang; end with a clear recommendation.
  • Essay (discursive): intro (state the issue) → arguments for → arguments against → conclusion with your view; formal register, no contractions; linkers: firstly, in addition, on the other hand, in conclusion.
  • Review (book/film/event): name what you review; para 1 = what it is + overall verdict; para 2 = key details (no full spoilers); para 3 = strengths and weaknesses; para 4 = recommendation + who would enjoy it; opinions must be supported.
All Exercise 6 tasks: 120–160 words, formal or semi-formal register — plan 3 minutes before you write.

• Read questions in the pause BEFORE each hearing; predict the answer type (a number? a name? a place?).
  • First hearing = answer; second hearing = CHECK, not start from zero.
  • Note-form answers must be spelled correctly; answers come in question order, so if you miss one, move on immediately.

• Part 1 warm-up (unmarked): short personal questions — relax and settle in.
  • Part 2 topic card: speak 1–2 minutes with structure: opinion → reason → example → personal experience.
  • Part 3 discussion: extend every answer (Answer–Extend–Example); disagree politely (“I see your point, but…”, “That's true, however…”). Fluency with a few mistakes beats silence.

• Read 15–20 minutes daily (quality news, features, short stories): underline unknown words, guess meaning from context first, then check — this builds the exact skill inference questions test.
  • Skim and scan drills: gist in 60 seconds (title + first/last line of each paragraph); scanning — find a name, date or number in a text as fast as possible.
  • Own-words drill: take one sentence from a text and rewrite it three different ways (synonyms, grammar changes) — comprehension marks depend on this.
  • Inference formula: “This suggests that … because the text says …” — always anchor an interpretation with a short quotation.
  • Mark-scheme study: after every past-paper attempt, read the mark scheme to learn how short, precise answers are phrased — 1 mark = 1 distinct point, never one point explained twice.
  • Summary cutting drill: reduce a 300-word passage to the word limit — delete examples, repetition, descriptions and figures of speech; keep only points that answer the focus line.

• Plan 3–5 minutes every time: bullet the task points, order them, decide the register (formal/informal) BEFORE writing — unplanned writing rambles and misses bullets.
  • Memorise one flexible skeleton per genre (see the FORMAT notes above) until you can reproduce it automatically — in the exam you spend your energy on ideas, not structure.
  • Weekly timed practice: one full task in exact exam time, then self-mark with a checklist: all bullets covered? register consistent? paragraphs linked? word count inside the limit?
  • Upgrade vocabulary deliberately: 5 new collocations per week in a notebook, and force them into your next practice piece (e.g. “a worthwhile experience”, “raise awareness”).
  • Vary sentence openings: fronted adverbials (“Surprisingly,…”, “Despite this,…”), mix short punchy sentences with longer complex ones — examiners reward controlled variety.
  • Keep an accuracy pass: reserve the last 3–4 minutes to check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, capital letters and end punctuation.
  • Rewrite, don't just re-read: get one piece marked each week and rewrite the SAME piece improved — rewriting is where the marks actually grow.

• Daily listening diet: 10–15 minutes of podcasts, news or lectures — first listen for gist, second for detail, third checking the transcript if available.
  • Predict before the recording starts: read every question in the pause, underline the question word (who/where/how many/why) and predict the answer type (a number? a name? a place?).
  • Two-hearing strategy: first hearing = write answers; second hearing = CHECK only. Never wait for the second hearing to start answering.
  • Beware distractors: speakers change their mind (“I was going to take the bus… but I drove”), correct numbers, and reject options before choosing. The first thing you hear is often NOT the answer.
  • Note-taking drill: practise writing key words only with abbreviations (info, bc, w/, →) — full sentences make you miss the next answer.
  • Spelling counts for names/places copied from the recording — they are usually spelled out letter by letter; write exactly what you hear.

How 0510 speaking works: your school chooses the route — Count-in Speaking (Component 5/6 counts toward the grade) or Speaking Endorsement (reported separately on the certificate). Ask your teacher which route you are on — the skills below are identical either way.

  • Daily 5-minute self-talk: pick any topic card, speak aloud non-stop — structure every answer as opinion → reason → example → personal experience.
  • Record yourself on your phone; replay and hunt for long pauses, repeated fillers (“um, like”), and problem sounds (th, v/w, p/b). Re-record until clean.
  • Build a phrase bank: opinions (“In my view…”, “I'm convinced that…”), polite disagreement (“I see your point, but…”, “That's true to an extent, however…”), buying time (“Well, let me think…”).
  • Never give one-word answers — extend everything (Answer–Extend–Example). A short answer with development beats a perfect sentence that says nothing.
  • Shadowing: play a podcast/news clip and repeat each sentence aloud immediately — this fixes rhythm, stress and intonation faster than reading.
  • Exam day: don't memorise speeches (examiners spot them instantly); speak naturally — small mistakes are fine if communication stays clear and fluent.

notes.b:
Everything in a computer is stored as binary (base 2) because circuits have two stable states (on/off). You must convert fluently between denary, binary and hexadecimal in both directions.

  • Denary → binary: repeated division by 2, read remainders upwards; or place values 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. Binary → denary: add the place values where a 1 sits.
  • Binary ↔ hex: split the byte into nibbles (4 bits) — each nibble is one hex digit (0–9, A=10 … F=15). E.g. 1011 0100 = B4.
  • Binary addition: 1+1 = 0 carry 1; 1+1+1 = 1 carry 1. An 8-bit register holding a result bigger than 255 causes an overflow error.
  • Why hex? shorter and less error-prone for humans: used in MAC/IP addresses, HTML colour codes (#FF8000), error codes and memory dumps.
  • Storage units (binary prefixes): bit → nibble (4) → byte (8) → KiB (1024 B) → MiB → GiB → TiB. Convert between units by multiplying/dividing by 1024 (or 8 for bits↔bytes).

• Text: each character has a binary code. ASCII = 7/8 bits (128–256 characters, English only); Unicode = 16+ bits, covers all world languages and emojis. Unicode files are larger than ASCII for the same text.
  • Sound: analogue waves are sampled at fixed intervals. Sample rate (samples per second, Hz) and sample resolution (bits per sample) both raise quality AND file size. File size ≈ sample rate × resolution × seconds × channels.
  • Images (bitmaps): a grid of pixels; resolution = pixels wide × high; colour depth = bits per pixel (8 bits = 256 colours). File size = width × height × colour depth ÷ 8 bytes. Vector graphics store drawing instructions instead — scale without pixelation, unsuitable for photos.

• Packets: data is split into packets — header (sender + destination IP, packet number) + payload + trailer (checksum/error check). Packets may take different routes and are reordered on arrival (packet switching).
  • Serial vs parallel: serial = one bit at a time over a single wire (slower per wire but reliable over long distances — USB is serial); parallel = many bits at once (fast only over short distances, suffers skew/interference).
  • Direction modes: simplex (one way only — keyboard→computer), half-duplex (both ways, not simultaneously — walkie-talkie), full-duplex (both ways at once — phone call).
  • Error detection: parity bit (extra bit makes number of 1s even/odd — fails if 2 errors); parity block (rows + columns locate the faulty bit); checksum (sum of bytes sent with data, recalculated on arrival); echo check (receiver sends data back for comparison — doubles traffic).
  • ARQ (automatic repeat request): receiver acknowledges each packet; sender re-transmits if no acknowledgement within a timeout.

Von Neumann architecture: instructions and data share the same memory and buses (stored-program concept).

  • CPU parts: Control Unit (decodes instructions, sends control signals), ALU (arithmetic + logic operations), registers — PC (holds address of NEXT instruction), MAR (address being read/written), MDR (data travelling to/from memory), ACC (stores ALU results).
  • Fetch–decode–execute cycle: PC address → MAR; instruction fetched along address/data bus into MDR; PC increments; CU decodes; instruction executed; repeat. Interrupts can pause the cycle.
  • Performance: more cores (parallel tasks), larger cache (ultra-fast on-CPU memory for frequently used data), higher clock speed (more cycles per second) all speed up processing.
  • RAM vs ROM: RAM is volatile (lost at power-off), read/write, holds running programs + data; ROM is non-volatile, read-only, holds the bootstrap/BIOS. Virtual memory: part of secondary storage used as overflow RAM — prevents crashes but is far slower (thrashing if overused).

• Know each device by USE, advantage and drawback: e.g. keyboard (text entry; slow for large volumes), mouse/touchscreen (direct manipulation), microphone (voice input/control), scanner/OCR (paper → editable text), barcode/QR reader (fast stock/product ID), sensor (automatic physical data — heat, light, pressure), biometric devices (fingerprint/face — secure ID).
  • Output: monitor (visual), printer — inkjet (home, cheap unit, costly ink), laser (offices, fast, cheap per page), 3D printer (prototypes, prosthetics); speakers; actuators (convert signals to movement — motors, valves in control systems).
  • Storage comparison: magnetic (HDD/tape — high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts = fragile + slower); optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray — portable, cheap, easily scratched, low capacity); solid-state (SSD/flash — no moving parts: fast, durable, more expensive per GB).
  • Cloud storage: access anywhere + easy sharing + off-site backup, but needs internet and raises privacy/subscription concerns.

• Application software does user tasks (browser, word processor); system software runs the machine (operating system, utilities, translators).
  • Operating system functions: managing memory, files, peripherals (drivers), users/security, multitasking (scheduling CPU time), and providing the user interface (GUI vs CLI).
  • Interrupts: signals (from hardware, e.g. printer out of paper, or software errors) that make the CPU pause its current task, service the interrupt, then resume — prioritised by importance.
  • High-level vs low-level languages: high-level (Python) is English-like, portable, one line → many machine instructions, needs translation; low-level (assembly/machine code) maps 1:1 to hardware, fast and memory-efficient, machine-specific, hard to write.
  • Translators: compiler translates the whole program at once into an executable (errors listed after; runs fast; source not needed to run); interpreter translates line-by-line each run (stops at the first error; easier debugging; slower); assembler translates assembly → machine code.

• Networks: LAN (one building/site, own hardware) vs WAN (wide area, uses third-party telecom lines); client-server (central server manages files/security — easy backups, single point of failure) vs peer-to-peer (equal machines — cheap, no central management).
  • Addressing: every device has a MAC address (fixed at manufacture, identifies the NIC) and an IP address (assigned for routing; static or dynamic). Routers forward packets between networks using IPs.
  • Internet ≠ WWW: the internet is the hardware/network infrastructure; the web is pages accessed via browsers using URLs and HTTP/HTTPS from web servers. Cookies store small user data/preferences (privacy implications).
  • Threats — know the differences: virus (attaches to a file, needs a host to spread), worm (self-replicates across networks alone), trojan (disguised as legitimate software), spyware/keylogger (records activity/keystrokes), ransomware (encrypts files for payment), adware; phishing (fake emails/sites harvesting details), pharming (redirecting to fake sites without a click), hacking (unauthorised access).
  • Defences: firewall (filters traffic in/out), anti-malware (scans/quarantines), authentication (passwords, biometrics, two-factor), access levels, encryption — symmetric encryption scrambles data so intercepted data is unreadable (HTTPS).

• Computational thinking: decomposition (break a problem into smaller sub-systems), abstraction (ignore irrelevant detail), pattern recognition, algorithm design.
  • Represent algorithms as flowcharts (terminator ovals, process rectangles, decision diamonds, input/output parallelograms) or pseudocode — be able to write BOTH from a problem description.
  • Standard algorithms to memorise: linear search; totalling and counting (running total in a loop); finding max/min/average; bubble sort (repeated passes swapping adjacent out-of-order items).
  • Trace tables: dry-run an algorithm line by line, recording every variable change — the standard way to find logic errors and predict output. Practise until flawless; this is guaranteed marks.
  • Validation (is data reasonable/possible?): presence, range, type, length, format checks and check digits. Verification (was it entered accurately?): double entry, visual check.
  • Test data: normal (accepted), abnormal/erroneous (rejected), extreme (largest/smallest acceptable) and boundary (just inside/outside a limit) — pick all four kinds when asked.

• Building blocks: variables (named, changeable), constants (fixed), data types — integer, real, char, string, Boolean. Sequence → selection (IF/ELSE, CASE) → iteration: count-controlled (FOR — repeats known times) vs condition-controlled (WHILE — pre-check, may run 0 times; REPEAT–UNTIL — post-check, runs at least once).
  • Totalling & counting inside loops; string handling (length, substring, upper/lower case, concatenation).
  • Arrays: indexed lists of one data type; read/write with loops (1D in Core; nested loops traverse 2D arrays in Supplement). Typical tasks: fill, search, find max, total, average.
  • Procedures & functions: named blocks that structure code; a function returns a value, a procedure does not; parameters pass data in. Local variables exist only inside their routine; global are visible everywhere (avoid unless necessary).
  • File handling: open → read/write → close (for storing data between runs, e.g. high scores).
  • Maintainable code: meaningful identifiers, comments, indentation/white space, modular routines — markers explicitly credit this.

• Flat-file database: one table; a field is one category of data, a record is one complete row, and the primary key uniquely identifies each record (must be unique + never blank).
  • SQL basics: SELECT field1, field2 FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY field ASC/DESC. Conditions use =, <>, >, <, AND/OR/NOT and wildcards (LIKE 'A%'). Also know SUM() and COUNT().
  • Logic gates: learn symbol + truth table for AND, OR, NOT, XOR (and NAND, NOR = inverted outputs). AND = both inputs 1; OR = at least one 1; XOR = inputs DIFFERENT.
  • Circuit skills (exam favourites): build a logic circuit from a written problem (e.g. “alarm sounds if door open AND key not turned, OR if window broken”), write the logic expression from a circuit, and complete a truth table for up to 3 inputs (2³ = 8 rows — always count them).

subjects.tag: P1 is theory (systems, networks, effects, applications, security, life cycle); P2 & P3 are timed PRACTICAL papers on document production, mail merge, databases, spreadsheets, presentations and web authoring. Computer-based exam: spreadsheet models (formulas, functions, charts) and web page creation with HTML/CSS. 2026–2028 syllabus format.

notes.b:
A computer system = hardware + software + data + users. Know the types of computer and their best uses: desktop (power, offices), laptop (portable work), tablet/smartphone (apps, communication), server (network services), mainframe (bulk processing — banks, census), embedded systems (single dedicated task inside washing machines, microwaves, cars — no keyboard/monitor).

  • Inside the case: CPU (processes instructions), motherboard, RAM (working memory — volatile), ROM (boot instructions — non-volatile), hard drive/SSD (long-term storage), graphics & sound cards, PSU, NIC (network interface).
  • Software split: applications (user tasks: word processor, browser) vs system software (operating system + utilities: antivirus, backup, disk defragmenter, compression).
  • OS functions: user interface (GUI/CLI), memory management, file management, security (user accounts/passwords), multitasking, managing peripherals via drivers.

notes.t: 2. Input & output devices — the exam favourites
notes.b:
• Direct data entry (know WHY each beats typing): barcode reader (fast, accurate stock/product ID), QR reader (links to websites/info), magnetic stripe reader (bank cards), chip & PIN / contactless (secure payment), RFID (tracking, passports), OMR (multiple-choice exam sheets), OCR (paper documents → editable text), MICR (bank cheques — magnetically readable even when stamped over), biometric systems (fingerprint/face/retina — unique, can't be forgotten or lent).
  • Sensors (for control/monitoring): temperature, light, pressure, moisture, motion, pH — they measure PHYSICAL quantities automatically and continuously; ADC converts analogue sensor signals to digital.
  • Manual input: keyboard, mouse, touchscreen (also output), microphone, scanner, digital camera, webcam, graphics tablet, joystick.
  • Output: monitor/TFT, inkjet (home/photos), laser (fast office volume, cheap per page), 3D printer (prototypes, prosthetics, model parts), speakers/headphones, projector, plotter (large accurate drawings), actuator (turns a signal into movement — motors, heaters, valves in control systems).

• Three technologies: magnetic (hard disk, tape — large capacity, low cost per GB; HDD has moving parts so slower + fragile; tape is cheap for archives/backups but serial access = slow to find data), optical (CD ~700 MB, DVD ~4.7 GB, Blu-ray ~25 GB — portable and cheap but scratchable; R = recordable once, RW = rewritable), solid state (SSD, memory cards, USB flash — no moving parts: fast, robust, tiny; costlier per GB).
  • Cloud storage: files on remote servers — access from any device, easy sharing, automatic off-site backup; drawbacks: needs internet, ongoing fees, data-privacy trust in the provider.
  • Capacity units: bit → byte (8 bits) → KB → MB → GB → TB (each ≈ 1000× the previous). Be ready to estimate: a photo ≈ a few MB, a film ≈ a few GB.
  • Choosing storage questions: justify using capacity needed, speed, portability, durability and cost per GB — always match to the scenario.

• LAN (one site, organisation owns the hardware) vs WAN (links distant sites using telecoms/satellite — e.g. bank branches); WLAN = wireless LAN (Wi-Fi). Benefits of networking: share files, printers, internet connection and software; central backup; communicate internally. Drawbacks: security risk, cost of servers/cabling, dependence on the network.
  • Internet vs intranet vs extranet: internet = public worldwide network; intranet = private, staff only; extranet = intranet extended to trusted partners/customers.
  • Communication applications: email (attachments, CC/BCC, mailing lists — asynchronous), instant messaging/chat, VoIP (voice over internet — cheap calls), video conferencing (meetings without travel — needs bandwidth; saves time/cost, reduces travel) and social networking. Know advantages + disadvantages of each in context.
  • Network security essentials: user IDs + passwords (strong password rules), access levels (read-only vs full), encryption of transmitted data, firewalls, and physical security of servers.

notes.t: 5. The effects of ICT — health, safety & employment
notes.b:
• Health problems from prolonged computer use (learn cause → prevention pairs): RSI in wrists/fingers (repetitive typing → ergonomic keyboard, wrist rests, breaks); back/neck strain (poor posture → adjustable chair, screen at eye level, footrest); eye strain/headaches (glare, long sessions → anti-glare screen, correct lighting, regular breaks, eye tests); deep vein thrombosis (sitting still → move regularly).
  • Safety hazards: trailing cables (trip → cable tidy/wireless), overloaded sockets (fire → one plug per socket), liquids near equipment, heavy CRT lifting.
  • Employment effects: automation removes routine/manual jobs but creates new ones (IT technicians, programmers, web designers); enables working from home (teleworking — less travel/cost, flexible hours, but isolation + distractions) and 24/7 global services.
  • Environment: e-waste toxins vs paperless offices and reduced commuting — argue both sides in 'discuss' questions.

• Banking: online banking (24/7 access, transfers, statements — vs fraud risk and branch closures), ATMs (chip & PIN, withdraw/deposit/balance), EFTPOS at checkouts, and how cheque processing uses MICR.
  • Shopping: e-commerce (global choice, price comparison, no travel — vs no try-before-buy, delivery waits, card fraud, fake sites); supermarkets use barcodes for automatic stock control (re-order levels) and loyalty cards (data mining shopping habits).
  • Education: online learning/CAL, virtual learning environments, video lessons — learn anywhere at your own pace; drawbacks: needs equipment/internet, less face-to-face support, distractions.
  • Health: patient record databases (shared instantly between doctors), computer-controlled prosthetics, tele-medicine (remote diagnosis), monitoring equipment (sensors + alarms free nurses for other duties — but no human judgement, can malfunction).
  • Control & monitoring: microprocessor-controlled devices (washing machines, traffic lights, burglar alarms): sensors → ADC → microprocessor compares with preset values → actuators respond. Know the loop for traffic lights and automatic greenhouses.
  • Government & media: online tax/census/e-voting debates, digital broadcasting, streaming.

• Threats to data: viruses/worms/trojans (spread via email attachments, downloads, USB sticks), hacking (unauthorised access), phishing (fake emails/sites tricking users into revealing details), spyware/keyloggers, ransomware, and accidental loss/deletion.
  • Countermeasures (match each to a threat): anti-virus/anti-malware kept UPDATED, firewalls, strong passwords + regular changes, two-factor authentication, biometrics, encryption (scrambles data — useless if intercepted), access levels, CCTV/locks for physical security, staff training (don't open unknown attachments), and regular BACKUPS stored off-site (grandfather–father–son rotation).
  • Data protection principles: personal data must be collected fairly, kept accurate and up to date, held no longer than needed, kept secure, used only for the stated purpose, and individuals can view/correct their data.
  • Computer misuse & copyright: hacking and spreading malware are criminal offences; software is protected by copyright — piracy = illegal copying; software licences define legal use (single-user, multi-user, site licence); plagiarism = passing off others' work as your own.

1. Analysis: identify the problem; investigate the CURRENT system (interviews, questionnaires, observation, document analysis); produce a requirements specification (hardware, software, inputs/outputs, processing).
  2. Design: data structures, input forms (with validation), output layouts, screen/report designs, file structures, test plan.
  3. Development & testing: build the system; test each module then the whole system with normal (accepted), abnormal (rejected) and extreme/boundary data; alpha testing (in-house) and beta testing (real users).
  4. Implementation — four strategies: direct changeover (old stops, new starts — cheap but risky), parallel running (both run together — safe, double workload), phased (part by part), pilot (one branch first).
  5. Documentation: technical documentation (for future programmers — data structures, flowcharts, code listings) and user documentation (how to install/use, screenshots, troubleshooting).
  6. Evaluation & maintenance: compare against the original requirements, gather user feedback, fix bugs and improve (perfective/adaptive/corrective maintenance).

notes.t: 9. Practical craft — document production & web authoring (P2/P3)
notes.b:
Exam context: you work to a printed brief against the clock — speed comes from knowing exactly where every feature lives.

  • Document production: page setup (margins, orientation, paper size), headers/footers (name/centre/candidate number — ALWAYS check the brief), fonts/styles applied consistently, bold/italic/underline, alignment, line spacing, bullets & numbering, tables (merge/split cells, borders), inserting and cropping images, text wrapping, columns, page/section breaks.
  • Mail merge: master document + data source → insert merge fields → filter/select recipients → merge to individual letters. Know the field codes shown in the brief and how to display data in required formats (dates, currency to 2 dp).
  • Web authoring: write simple HTML by hand: structure tags (<html>, <head>, <title>, <body>), headings <h1>–<h3>, paragraphs <p>, hyperlinks <a href>, images <img src> (with alt text), tables <table><tr><td>, lists <ul><li>. Test that links/images actually work — evidence screenshots go in your submission.

• Databases: create tables with correct data types (text, number, date, currency, yes/no) and a primary key; validation rules (range checks, input masks, required fields); queries with criteria on one or more fields (=, >, <, AND/OR, wildcards LIKE '*text*'), sorting, calculated fields (e.g. total = price × qty), then present as forms (easy data entry) and grouped/sorted reports with headings, totals and counts.
  • Spreadsheets: formulas always start with = ; core functions SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT/COUNTA, IF(condition, true, false), VLOOKUP, and nested functions; relative vs absolute referencing ($A$1 stays fixed when copied — used for tax rates/multipliers); replicate formulas down; format cells (2 dp, currency, %); named ranges; charts (choose the right type — bar for comparison, line for trends, pie for proportions — with titles and axis labels).
  • Presentations: master slide (logo/title on every slide), consistent colour scheme/font, concise bullet points, images, transitions between slides and animation effects on objects, slide numbers and footer, audience handouts. Import data from other packages (chart from a spreadsheet, table from a database).
  • Golden rule for P2/P3: read the brief twice, do the tasks in the order given, and screenshot/print every piece of evidence requested — marks are lost for missing evidence, not missing knowledge.

Practical papers are marked on output evidence: exact file names, visible formulas, field properties and screenshots of criteria. Save files exactly as instructed and screenshot formulas where asked.

Phishing: fake emails/sites trick users into revealing credentials. Pharming: traffic silently redirected to a fake site without an email lure.

Old and new systems run together until the new one proves reliable — safe but duplicated effort/cost.

solved.q: A courier company wants drivers to record deliveries with signatures. Suggest suitable input devices and justify two choices.
steps: Identify the need: mobile, robust, capture signature + barcode.
Touchscreen for signature capture — direct, no extra hardware.
Barcode/QR scanner — fast, accurate parcel ID.
Reject keyboard: slow and impractical on the move.
solved.a: Touchscreen + built-in scanner, justified in context.

solved.q: Cell D2 holds hours worked; F1 holds the hourly rate. Write the pay formula in E2 so it can be copied down 50 rows.

notes.b:
• DEAD CLIC: Debits = Expenses, Assets, Drawings. Credits = Liabilities, Income, Capital.
  • Every transaction: one debit + one equal credit. Cash book, petty cash book (imprest!), sales/purchases journals → ledgers.

• Trial balance checks arithmetic, NOT all errors — omission, commission, original entry, complete reversal, principle errors DON'T show; single-sided errors DO (suspense account).
  • Correct via journal + suspense until it clears.

• Updated cash book first (direct debits, bank charges, credit transfers, dishonoured cheques).
  • Then reconciliation statement: balance per bank ± unpresented cheques ± uncredited deposits → adjusted.

• Sales ledger control = trade receivables; purchases ledger control = trade payables.
  • Contra entries appear on BOTH control accounts. Credit sales→debit SLCA; receipts→credit SLCA.

• Straight line: (cost − residual) ÷ life. Reducing balance: net book value × %.
  • Accruals (owed, add), prepayments (paid early, deduct), irrecoverable debts (expense), provision for doubtful debts (% of receivables).
  • CapEx vs RevExp: improving/extending = capital; repairs/running = revenue.

• Income statement: revenue − COGS = gross profit − expenses = profit for the year.
  • SOFP: non-current assets (at NBV) + current assets − current liabilities = net current assets; + capital − drawings + profit.
  • Also know: partnerships (appropriation account!), limited companies (share capital, debentures, dividends), clubs (receipts & payments + subscriptions), manufacturing (prime cost → factory overheads → cost of production).

• Mark-up (on cost) vs margin (on selling): margin = m/(100+m). ROCE = operating profit ÷ capital employed. Current ratio = CA:CL. Acid test removes inventory.
  • Always say what the ratio MEASURES and judge using another business/industry comparison.

subjects.fmt: How P2 questions come: Scenario-led: 'Kamran owns a shop…' then structured parts — (a) journal entries, (b) extract the corrected account, (c) prepare the income statement for the year, (d) calculate and comment on two ratios. Working marks are real marks: wrong figure but correct method still earns. Own-figure rule: later parts using your earlier (wrong) answer get credited. Show every calculation. flash.a: Debits: Expenses, Assets, Drawings. Credits: Liabilities, Income, Capital.

flash.q: Straight line vs reducing balance depreciation?
flash.a: SL: (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life (same each year). RB: net book value × fixed % (higher early, lower later).

flash.q: Which errors does the trial balance NOT reveal?
flash.a: Omission, commission, original entry, complete reversal, principle — anything affecting both sides equally.
Explains the difference between cash book and bank statement — timing (unpresented cheques, uncredited deposits) and errors.
Markup is % on COST; margin is % on SELLING price. margin = markup/(100+markup).
(Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities — tests ability to pay debts without selling stock.

solved.q: Revenue $84,000; purchases $52,000; opening inventory $6,000; closing inventory $8,000; rent paid $5,500 including $500 prepaid; wages $9,000; depreciation on equipment (cost $20,000, 10% straight line). Prepare extracts. [8]
steps: Rent expense = 5,500 − 500 (prepayment) = 5,000.
Depreciation = 10% × 20,000 = 2,000.
solved.a: Profit = $18,000. Each adjustment you handle = 1–2 marks.

solved.q: Cash book shows $2,400 debit. Bank statement shows $1,900. Unpresented cheques $700; uncredited deposits $200; bank charges $50 in statement only. Reconcile.
steps: Update cash book: −50 bank charges → cash book = 2,350.
Reconciliation: balance per bank statement 1,900 + uncredited deposits 200 − unpresented cheques 700 = 1,400?? — check direction: adjusted bank balance = 1,900 − 700 + 200 = 1,400.

Discrepancy → also check: cheques paid in not yet credited are ADDED to the bank side... correct approach: corrected cash book 2,350 must equal 1,400 + timing items rearranged: 1,400 + 700 − 200 = 1,900 ✓. If cash book is 2,350, there is a $950 error elsewhere — exam answers usually reconcile fully; here the lesson: always update the cash book FIRST, then balance.
solved.a: Method marks: update cash book first, then reconciliation statement with unpresented cheques and uncredited deposits as timing differences.

practice.q: 4. Why is a provision for doubtful debts made?
practice.a: Prudence — receivables may not all be collected; match the estimated loss to the period of sale, showing receivables at a realistic value.

notes.t: P1 History — the story in one line
notes.b:
• 1857: War of Independence — causes (greased cartridges, doctrine of lapse, missionary activity), failure (no unity, limited spread, no modern leadership), consequences (Mughal rule ends, British Crown takes over, Muslims blamed & sidelined).
  • Sir Syed: Two-Nation theory seeds; Aligarh Movement; scientific education for Muslims; loyalist politics after 1857; Hindi-Urdu controversy (1867) turned him to Muslim nationalism.
  • 1906: Simla Deputation → Muslim League founded (Aga Khan, Nawab Salimullah); separate electorates 1909.
  • 1913–28: Lucknow Pact (1916) — Hindu-Muslim unity; Khilafat Movement (1919–24) — mass Muslim politicisation; Nehru Report (1928) rejections → Jinnah's 14 Points (1929).
  • 1930–40: Iqbal's Allahabad Address (1930) — separate Muslim state in NW; Round Table Conferences fail; 1937 Congress rule reveals Hindu majoritarianism; Lahore/Pakistan Resolution (23 March 1940).
  • 1940–47: Cripps (1942), Gandhi-Jinnah talks (1944), Simla Conference (1945), Cabinet Mission (1946) — 3-tier federation rejected by Congress; Direct Action Day (16 Aug 1946); Interim government; 3 June 1947 Plan → Independence 14 August 1947.

• Early problems: refugees, water (canal water dispute), assets division, Kashmir war (1948), assassination of Liaquat Ali Khan (1951).
  • Constitutions: 1956 (first, parliamentary, Islamic Republic), 1962 (Ayub — presidential, Basic Democracies), 1973 (parliamentary, federal, Islamic provisions; still current).
  • Regimes: Ayub (1958–69, growth but inequality → 1968-69 movement), Yahya (1969–71 → 1971 war & Bangladesh), Bhutto (1971–77, 1973 constitution, nationalisation, Simla Agreement, nuclear programme start), Zia (1977–88, Islamisation, Afghan war), 1988–99 democratic alternation (Benazir/Nawaz), Musharraf (1999–2008), return to democracy 2008+.
  • Economy & society: agriculture reforms, industrialisation, education movements.

• Global community: Kashmir dispute & UN; relations with India (wars 1948, 1965, 1971, Kargil 1999), China (all-weather: Karakoram Highway, CPEC), USA (SEATO/CENTO to post-9/11), Afghanistan & Soviet war, Muslim world (OIC, Arab-Israeli issues, Iran, Saudi), SAARC, UN peacekeeping.
  • Society & culture: Urdu as national language & regional languages; religion & religious minorities; arts, media, sports (cricket, hockey, squash); regional cultures; women in society.

• Location: 24°N–37°N, 61°E–77°E; borders (India E, Afghanistan W/NW — Durand Line, Iran SW, China NE — highest border at Khunjerab).
  • Landforms: northern mountains (K2, Nanga Parbat, Karakoram, Himalaya, Hindu Kush — collision of Indo-Australian & Eurasian plates), western highlands (Sulaiman, Kirthar), Potohar & Salt Range, Indus plain, Balochistan plateaus, coastal areas.
  • Indus system: Indus + Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej (tributaries); eastern rivers given to India, western to Pakistan under Indus Waters Treaty 1960 (World Bank).
  • Resources: minerals (coal Sindh, chromite, gypsum, limestone, oil/gas), forests (coniferous north, mangroves Indus delta), fisheries (Karachi), agriculture land.

• Climate: continental, arid/semi-arid; monsoon (Jul–Sep, from Bay of Bengal), western depressions (Dec–Mar), tropical cyclones (Arabian Sea, May–Jun & Oct–Nov). Floods 2010/2022, droughts in Thar/Cholistan.
  • Climate change: causes (GHG, deforestation); impacts for Pakistan (glacial melt — GLOF, sea intrusion in Indus delta, heatwaves, floods); responses: mitigation (reforestation — Billion Tree Tsunami, renewable energy) & adaptation (early warning, flood management, resilient crops). NEW syllabus case-study element.

notes.t: P2 — Population, urbanisation, quality of life
notes.b:
• Population: ~240 million (5th largest); growth rate ~1.6–2%; youthful pyramid; density highest in Punjab; migration (rural→urban push-pull; Afghan refugees; emigration to Gulf).
  • Urbanisation: Karachi (~17M, largest, port, problems: water, sanitation, transport, katchi abadis), Lahore, Faisalabad, Islamabad; causes (jobs, services); responses: planned schemes (e.g. Khuda Ki Basti model), katchi abadi upgrading.
  • Quality of life: HDI indicators; literacy ~58%; healthcare access; poverty; government's role (Benazir Income Support, health cards).

• Agriculture: ~20% GDP, ~37% employment; crops — cotton (textiles backbone), rice (Basmati exports), wheat, sugarcane; livestock largest agri sub-sector; irrigation: world's largest canal system, also tubewells, karez (Balochistan); problems: waterlogging/salinity, low yields, fragmentation.
  • Industry: textiles (60%+ of exports), cement, fertiliser, sports goods (Sialkot), surgical instruments, IT growing; cottage vs large-scale.
  • Energy: mix (gas, oil, hydel, coal Thar, nuclear, solar/wind); crisis causes (circular debt, transmission losses, demand growth); CPEC energy projects.
  • Trade: exports (textiles, rice, leather, sports goods) vs imports (oil, machinery, edible oil) → trade deficit; partners: USA, China, UAE, EU; remittances major inflow; tourism potential (northern areas).

flash.a: Pressure reversal: summer low over land draws moist SW winds from the Bay of Bengal; blocked by Himalayas → heavy rain July–September.
Underground channel tapping groundwater to the surface — ancient irrigation in Balochistan, avoids evaporation.
China-Pakistan Economic Corridor: ~$60bn infrastructure/energy network (roads, Gwadar port, power plants) linking Gwadar to Xinjiang.

solved.q: 'How successful was Ayub Khan's government (1958–69)?'
steps: Intro: context — Ayub took over in 1958 coup; judge by economy, stability, foreign policy, then cost.
Successes: Green Revolution growth (~6% GDP), Indus Waters Treaty 1960, 1962 constitution, alliance diplomacy (CENTO/SEATO aid), infrastructure (Tarbela/Mangla).
Failures: 1965 war drained economy, inequality & 22 families criticism, no political freedom, 1968–69 mass uprising forced resignation.
Verdict: economically progressive but politically repressive — short-term stability bought at the price of the system's legitimacy.
solved.a: Balance + case examples + verdict = top band. In the NEW format, the same content fits the extended-response part of a 25-mark question.

solved.q: Resources show a village suffering floods yearly: options — (A) build embankments, (B) relocate village, (C) early-warning + raised homes. Recommend one. [6]
steps: Option A: protects farmland & homes; costly; embankments can fail catastrophically (2010).
Option B: permanent safety; destroys community/livelihoods; very costly; culturally disruptive.
Option C: cheapest, protects lives quickly; doesn't protect farmland fully.
Verdict: C now + A phased — because lives first (prudence), funds limited (resource says poor district), community stays intact.
solved.a: The verdict must weigh at least two options against the resource's facts.

practice.a: Doctrine of Lapse & annexations; interference in religion (missionaries, 1850 law); discrimination in jobs/army; economic exploitation (land revenue, deindustrialisation); any four.

notes.b:
• Scarcity: unlimited wants meet limited resources → choice is unavoidable → every choice has an opportunity cost (the next best alternative given up).
  • Factors of production: land (rent), labour (wages), capital (interest), enterprise (profit).
  • Production possibility curve (PPC): points inside = unemployed resources; on the curve = maximum efficiency; outside = currently unattainable; an outward shift = economic growth.
  • Specialisation and division of labour raise output but create interdependence and over-specialisation risk.

• Market, planned and mixed economic systems; the market allocates through the price mechanism.
  • Demand curves slope down, supply curves slope up; equilibrium is where they cross. A price change causes an extension/contraction along a curve; a non-price factor shifts the whole curve.
  • PED = %Δ quantity demanded ÷ %Δ price; elastic > 1, inelastic < 1 — PED shapes how price changes hit revenue and how taxes are shared.
  • Government intervention: maximum and minimum prices, indirect taxes, subsidies, regulation, quotas, direct provision — each creates winners, losers and possible distortions.

• Money's functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payment.
  • Central bank: issues currency, sets the policy interest rate, supervises banks. Commercial banks: take deposits, lend, create credit.
  • Households: spending, saving and borrowing respond to income, interest rates, confidence, age and culture.
  • Workers weigh wage and non-wage factors; firms choose between aims such as profit, growth, survival and market share.

• Macroeconomic aims: economic growth, low unemployment, stable prices, balance of payments stability, redistribution of income, environmental sustainability — aims can conflict.
  • Fiscal policy = government spending + taxation; a budget deficit means spending exceeds revenue.
  • Monetary policy = interest rates, money supply, exchange-rate tools. Supply-side policy = education and training, labour-market reform, deregulation, privatisation, incentives.
  • Inflation (CPI-measured): demand-pull vs cost-push causes; hurts savers and lenders, helps borrowers. Recession: falling GDP, rising unemployment.

• Living standards: real GDP per head and the Human Development Index (HDI) — each has advantages and blind spots.
  • Absolute poverty (below a minimum income line) vs relative poverty (far below average income in that country).
  • Population change = birth rate, death rate and net migration; population pyramids are read, not drawn; the optimum population concept.
  • Development gaps come from differences in income, productivity, sector sizes (primary/secondary/tertiary), saving, investment, education and healthcare.

• Specialisation between countries and the gains from free trade; protectionism via tariffs and quotas — winners and losers.
  • Multinational companies (MNCs): jobs, investment and technology vs profit outflow and influence over governments.
  • Foreign exchange rates: floating vs fixed systems; depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer.
  • Current account of the balance of payments = trade in goods + trade in services + primary income + secondary income; causes and consequences of deficits and surpluses.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come (Paper 2): Section A is a compulsory data-response question — read the source, quote figures, and calculate when asked (PED, inflation, deficits). Section B questions climb from Define/State (2 marks) through Explain (4–6 marks, chain of reasoning) to Discuss (8 marks, levels of response). For 8-mark part (d) answers: develop two sides with separate reasoning (never mirror statements), then finish with a justified judgement ('it depends on…'). Calculators are allowed in both papers; diagrams must be fully labelled.

flash.a: The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.

flash.q: Name the four factors of production and their rewards.
flash.a: Land (rent), labour (wages), capital (interest), enterprise (profit).

flash.q: PED formula and what elastic demand means.
flash.a: PED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP. Elastic (PED > 1): quantity responds more than proportionally to price.

flash.q: Extension vs shift of a demand curve?
flash.a: A price change moves along the curve (extension/contraction); a non-price factor shifts the whole curve.

flash.q: Difference between fiscal and monetary policy?
flash.a: Fiscal = government spending and taxation; monetary = interest rates, money supply and exchange-rate tools.
Demand-pull: too much spending pulls prices up. Cost-push: rising production costs (wages, imports) push prices up.
Trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income.

flash.q: What does HDI add that GDP per head misses?
flash.a: Health (life expectancy) and education (schooling) — GDP per head only measures average income.

solved.q: A bus company raises fares by 10% and journeys fall from 50 000 to 40 000 per week. Calculate the PED for bus travel and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic. [3]
steps: PED = −20% ÷ 10% = −2 → use absolute value 2.
PED = 2 > 1, so demand is price elastic — revenue falls after the fare rise.
solved.a: PED = 2 (elastic). Full marks need both percentage changes and the interpretation.

solved.q: Discuss whether a government should subsidise public transport. [8]
steps: Side A: lower fares → higher ridership → less congestion and pollution; helps low-income households (affordability).
Side B: subsidy costs taxpayers and may crowd out other spending; firms may become inefficient if guaranteed revenue; effect depends on PED and quality of alternatives.
Judgement: worth it where roads are congested and demand is price elastic; less effective where service quality, not price, is the binding constraint.
solved.a: Two developed sides + a reasoned judgement reach Level 3 (6–8 marks); one-sided answers cap at Level 2.

practice.q: 1. A student chooses a part-time job paying $40 over studying for an extra hour. What is the opportunity cost of the job? [2]
practice.a: The extra hour of study (the next best alternative given up) — not the $40, which is gained.

practice.q: 2. The CPI rises from 120 to 126 in one year. Calculate the inflation rate. [2]
3. Explain one effect of a fall in the exchange rate on the current account. [3]
practice.a: Exports become cheaper and imports dearer for foreign buyers → export demand rises and import demand falls (if demand is price elastic) → the current account deficit shrinks / surplus grows.

practice.q: 4. State two supply-side policies a government could use to raise economic growth. [2]
practice.a: Any two of: education and training, labour-market reforms, lower direct taxes as incentives, deregulation, privatisation.

flash.a: a² = b² + c² − 2bc·cosA.
a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC.

Σ(fx) ÷ Σf using class midpoints.

solved.q: Solve: x + y = 7, x² + y² = 25.
steps: Pairs: (3,4) and (4,3).

solved.q: In a circle, triangle ABC has AB as diameter, C on circumference, AC = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm. Find the radius.
steps: Angle in semicircle: ∠ACB = 90°.
AB² = 6² + 8² = 100 → AB = 10 cm.
Radius = 5 cm.

practice.q: 1. Factorise fully: 6x² − 7x − 20.
2. A = {factors of 12}, B = {prime numbers < 12}. Find n(A ∩ B).

papers.d: Qur'an, Hadith, pillars & articles of faith, Prophet's life (Makkah/Madinah periods), khilafah of the four rightly-guided caliphs.
Application of teachings to modern situations; Islamic law (Sharia sources: Qur'an, Sunnah, ijma, qiyas); family & social ethics.

notes.b: Six articles: Allah, angels, revealed books, prophets, Day of Judgement, divine decree (qadar). Five pillars with details of each (zakah rates/nisab, sawm rules, hajj rites order).
Revelation & compilation (Abu Bakr's collection, Uthman's standard codex); themes of key surahs studied in syllabus; science of Hadith (isnad, matn); difference between Qur'an and Hadith.

Makkah period: early revelations, boycott, Taif, Isra & Miraj, pledges of Aqabah. Madinah period: Hijrah (first year of Islamic calendar, 622 CE), Constitution of Madinah, battles (Badr, Uhud, Khandaq, Hunayn, Tabuk), conquest of Makkah (630 CE), Farewell Sermon.
Abu Bakr (wars of apostasy, compilation of Qur'an), Umar (expansion, administration: hijri calendar, diwan), Uthman (standard codex, naval expansion, martyrdom), Ali (first fitna, arbitration).
Sources: Qur'an → Sunnah → Ijma (consensus) → Qiyas (analogy). Examples of application: interest (riba) & banking, modesty & dress, honesty in trade, family law, jihad vs terrorism misconception.

subjects.fmt: How questions come: P1 = descriptive ('Describe the events of...', 'Explain the importance of...') — names, dates, sequence. P2 = applied: a modern scenario (e.g., a Muslim student facing exam pressure/dishonest friend) answered with RELEVANT Qur'an/Hadith references and practical advice. Learn 2–3 Qur'anic quotes or Hadith per topic.

flash.q: First year of the Islamic calendar?
flash.a: 622 CE — the year of the Hijrah (migration to Madinah).

flash.q: Four sources of Sharia in order?
flash.a: Qur'an, Sunnah (Hadith), Ijma (consensus), Qiyas (analogy).

flash.q: What happened at the First Pledge of Aqabah?
flash.a: 12 men from Yathrib pledged faith & obedience — first allegiance before the Hijrah.

flash.q: Who compiled the Qur'an into one book, and who made the standard codex?
flash.a: Abu Bakr ordered the collection after Yamamah; Caliph Uthman produced the standard codex sent to the provinces.

solved.q: 'A Muslim shopkeeper is tempted to hide defects in goods to make sales. Using Islamic teachings, advise him.' [10]
steps: Honesty in trade is commanded — the Prophet said 'The truthful merchant is with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs.'
Deception (ghish) invalidates a sale's blessing — Qur'an condemns fraud (mutaffifin).
Practical advice: disclose defects, fair weights & measures, accept returns; reputation brings barakah.
Conclusion: short-term gain vs long-term reward — taqwa and customer trust win.
solved.a: Teachings (Qur'an/Hadith quoted) + applied advice + conclusion = full marks.

practice.q: 1. Give four events of the Madinah period in chronological order.
practice.a: Hijrah & mosque building → Battle of Badr (624) → Uhud (625) → Khandaq (627) → Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628) → conquest of Makkah (630) → Farewell Sermon (632).

practice.q: 2. What was the Constitution of Madinah?
practice.a: Agreement between Muslims, Jews & pagans of Madinah forming one ummah with mutual defence & religious freedom — first written constitution of a plural state.
