papers.d: Quadratics, functions, coordinate geometry, circular measure, trigonometry, series, differentiation, integration.
AS pure: algebra, logarithms/exponentials, trigonometric identities, differentiation & integration techniques.
A2 pure: algebra (partial fractions), logarithms, trigonometry, differentiation (parametric, implicit), integration (by parts, substitutions), differential equations, vectors.
Forces & equilibrium, kinematics of motion in a line, Newton's laws, energy/work/power, momentum.
Permutations/combinations, probability, discrete random variables, binomial & geometric distributions, continuous random variables, normal distribution.

notes.b: Factor/remainder theorem; sketching curves & transformations; arithmetic/geometric progressions (S∞ = a/(1−r)); binomial expansion for any rational n; log laws (solve e.g. 2^x = 5 → x = ln5/ln2).

Chain/product/quotient rules; stationary points (second derivative test); integration by substitution & parts (∫u dv = uv − ∫v du); definite integrals = area under curve; volume of revolution; separable differential equations with initial conditions.

Identities (sin² + cos² = 1, tan = sin/cos); solve trig equations giving FULL general solutions; R-formulae (a cosθ + b sinθ = R cos(θ−α)); vector line equations r = a + λb, intersection, perpendicularity (dot product = 0).
Resolve forces; F = ma along lines; SUVAT with calculus (v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt); connected particles & pulleys; work-energy & power P = Fv; momentum conservation in 1D.
P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B); conditional probability; Binomial B(n,p): mean np, variance npq; Normal distribution: standardise z = (X−μ)/σ; normal approximations to binomial (np>5, nq>5).

subjects.fmt: How questions come: 10–11 structured questions escalating in demand; later parts use earlier answers (error carried forward). Method marks dominate — a correct integral set up earns most marks even if arithmetic slips. Trig equation answers need the general solution (nπ + ...) unless a range is given. Stats papers mix a ~6-mark normal-distribution calculation with short probability items.

flash.a: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du (choose u by LIATE).

flash.q: Sum to infinity of geometric series?
flash.a: S∞ = a/(1−r), valid only when |r| < 1.
z = (X − μ)/σ — converts normal values to standard normal tables.
dy/dx = 0; classify with d²y/dx²: >0 min, <0 max (or sign test of dy/dx).

flash.q: General solution of sin x = sin α?
flash.a: x = nπ + (−1)ⁿα for integer n.

solved.q: Find the area enclosed by y = x(4 − x) and the x-axis.
steps: Curve crosses x-axis at x = 0 and x = 4.
Area = ∫₀⁴ (4x − x²) dx = [2x² − x³/3]₀⁴.

practice.q: 1. Solve 3^(2x) = 7, giving x to 3 s.f.
2. A ball is projected vertically at 19.6 m/s. Find max height. (g = 9.8)
3. In a binomial B(20, 0.3), find mean and variance.
practice.a: mean = np = 6; variance = npq = 4.2.

subjects.tag: AS = P1+P2 (+P3 practical); full A Level adds P4 + P5. Mechanisms and multi-step calculations separate A from E.

papers.d: 40 MCQs on all AS topics including calculations. Full A Level weighting shown; AS-only weighting is 31%.
Short structured items: definitions, bonding explanations, moles/energetics/kinetics/equilibrium calculations. Full A Level weighting shown; AS-only weighting is 46%.
Laboratory-based Advanced Practical Skills paper; this is not an Alternative to Practical route. Weight shown is for the full A Level.
Deeper physical chemistry (thermodynamics, kinetics, equilibrium, electrochemistry), inorganic trends, organic synthesis & analysis.
Separate written Planning, Analysis and Evaluation paper; it does not replace Paper 3. Weight shown is for the full A Level.

notes.b:
• Hess's law cycles & bond enthalpies; ΔH = mcΔθ calorimetry with heat loss corrections.
  • Rate equations & orders (initial rates method), rate constant k, Arrhenius (ln k vs 1/T graph), activation energy.
  • Kc & Kp with ICE tables; Le Chatelier; Haber/Birkeland–Eyde context.
  • E° cells & feasibility (ΔG = −nFE), electrolysis quantities (Q = It, moles = Q/nF).

• Group 2: trends in reactivity, solubility of sulfates/hydroxides, flame colours & uses.
  • Group 17: oxidising power down, displacement reactions, halide tests, bleach chemistry.
  • Transition metals: d-block configurations, variable oxidation states, coloured ions (d-electron transitions), catalysts (Fe in Haber, V₂O₅ in Contact), complex ions & ligand exchange.

• Homologous families with reactions: alkanes(free-radical substitution) → alkenes(electrophilic addition, mechanism with curly arrows!) → alcohols → carbonyls(nucleophilic addition) → carboxylic acids → esters.
  • Learn mechanisms as electron stories: curly arrow FROM lone pair/π bond TO electron-deficient atom.
  • Isomerism: structural, E/Z (CIP priority rules), optical.
  • Identification: IR (O–H broad 3230–3550, C=O 1700), mass spec (molecular ion, fragments like m/z 15 CH₃), ¹³C/¹H NMR (chemical shift, integration, splitting n+1).
  • Synthesis routes: how to convert A→B in ≤4 steps (e.g. ethene → ethanoic acid; benzene → phenylamine).

subjects.fmt: How P4 comes: data-driven physical questions (calculate Kc from a table of moles; sketch Ea on a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution after catalyst added), inorganic trend questions ('explain why...' — use size/charge/electronic structure), and organic multi-part synthesis with mechanisms drawn for key steps. P5 gives raw experimental data and asks you to plot ln k vs 1/T, determine gradient = −Ea/R, and evaluate the experiment's precision.

flash.a: Arrow shows electron PAIR movement: from a lone pair or bond → towards an electron-deficient atom. Never from positive atoms.
Power of a concentration in the rate equation; found by initial-rates experiments (varying one concentration at a time).
A system at equilibrium counteracts imposed changes (concentration, pressure, temperature) — but catalyst does NOT shift position.
n equivalent neighbouring H → signal splits into n+1 peaks (doublet, triplet, quartet...).

flash.q: What makes transition metals good catalysts?
flash.a: Variable oxidation states let them donate/accept electrons in steps, and d-orbitals adsorb reactants on their surface.
A positive E° cell → negative ΔG → feasible reaction.

solved.q: A + B ⇌ C + D. Start 1.0 mol each of A and B in 1 dm³; equilibrium [C] = 0.60 mol/dm³. Find Kc.
steps: Change: −0.6 for A, B; +0.6 for C, D.

solved.q: Describe the mechanism for propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane (major).
steps: HBr polarised: Hδ⁺ attacks π bond — curly arrow π → H; π electrons form C–H bond.
Carbocation intermediate forms (secondary here — more stable).
Arrow from Br⁻ lone pair to carbocation carbon → product.
Markovnikov: H adds to carbon with more H already (secondary carbocation preferred).
solved.a: Two curly-arrow steps; intermediate = carbocation; major product = 2-bromopropane.

practice.q: 1. Calculate ΔH for a reaction given: bond breaking totals 4360 kJ/mol, bond forming totals 4820 kJ/mol.
practice.a: ΔH = broken − formed = 4360 − 4820 = −460 kJ/mol (exothermic).

practice.q: 2. Why is Mg(OH)₂ more soluble than Ba(OH)₂? Explain the trend.
practice.a: Down Group 2, larger cation → lower charge density → less polarisation of the O–H bond → easier to separate ions → hydroxide solubility increases. Wait — actually Group 2 hydroxide solubility INCREASES down: Mg(OH)₂ insoluble, Ba(OH)₂ soluble. Check direction!

practice.q: 3. State the trend in oxidising power of halogens down Group 17 and why.
practice.a: Decreases down the group: larger atom, more shielding → outer electrons further from nucleus → harder to gain an electron (weaker attraction).

practice.q: 4. An ester shows a C=O stretch at 1740 cm⁻¹ but no broad O–H band. What does this tell you?
practice.a: Ester confirmed: carbonyl present (1740) and absence of broad 3230–3550 cm⁻¹ rules out carboxylic acid.

subjects.tag: AS = P1+P2 (+P3 practical); A2 = P4 + P5. Definitions must be word-perfect.

papers.d: 40 MCQs incl. unit analysis and estimation. Full A Level weighting shown; AS-only weighting is 31%.
Kinematics, dynamics, work/energy, momentum, matter, waves, electricity. Full A Level weighting shown; AS-only weighting is 46%.
Laboratory-based Advanced Practical Skills paper; this is not an Alternative to Practical route. Weight shown is for the full A Level.
Circular motion, gravitation, SHM, thermal physics, electric/gravitational/magnetic fields, capacitors, nuclear physics, medical physics.
Separate written Planning, Analysis and Evaluation paper; it does not replace Paper 3. Weight shown is for the full A Level.

notes.b: Projectile motion (independent x/y); Newton's 2nd in momentum form F = Δp/Δt; conservation of momentum & energy in collisions (elastic vs inelastic).
a = v²/r = ω²r towards centre; satellites: GMm/r² = mv²/r, orbital speed v = √(GM/r); g = GM/r². SHM: a = −ω²x, T = 2π√(m/k), T = 2π√(L/g) for pendulum; energy exchange KE↔PE.

• Gravitational: g = F/m, potential φ = −GM/r, field lines never cross.
  • Electric: F = kQ₁Q₂/r², E = V/d, capacitors C = Q/V, energy ½QV, series/parallel, RC discharge (log graphs).
  • Magnetic: F = BILsinθ, F = Bqv, circular path of charged particle r = mv/qB; induction ε = −dΦ/dt; transformers ideal (VpIp = VsIs).

pV = nRT; internal energy = sum of KE+PE of particles; specific heat & latent heat experiments. Radioactivity: N = N₀e^(−λt), half-life = ln2/λ; binding energy & mass defect E = mc²; fission vs fusion; background & safety.

subjects.fmt: How questions come: P2 builds one scenario across parts (e.g., ball thrown → velocity → momentum → energy → power). 'Define' questions demand precise wording ('the rate of change of momentum...'). P4 loves derivations (show T² = 4π²m/k) and ratio reasoning. P5 asks you to design an experiment (identify independent/dependent variables, control two variables, describe graph treatment including log-linear to find constants).

flash.a: Acceleration ∝ displacement and directed TOWARDS the equilibrium point (a = −ω²x).
Towards the centre — it is NOT a new force; it's the resultant of real forces (tension, gravity, friction).
VpIp = VsIs — step-up voltage means step-down current (hence less I²R heat loss).
Energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1 volt = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
t½ = ln2/λ.

solved.q: A satellite orbits at height where g = 8.7 m/s² (radius r). Find orbital speed if r = 6.9 × 10⁶ m.
steps: Gravity provides centripetal force: mg = mv²/r.

solved.q: A 470 μF capacitor charged to 12 V. Find stored energy.

practice.q: 1. A 0.5 kg mass on a spring (k = 200 N/m) oscillates. Find the period.
2. Define electric field strength and give its unit.
practice.a: Force per unit positive charge (E = F/Q); unit N/C (or V/m).

practice.q: 3. An alpha particle (2 protons) and a beta particle (1 electron) enter the same magnetic field at equal speed. Whose path curves more tightly, and why?
practice.a: Beta: r = mv/qB — equal v, beta has far smaller mass and half the charge magnitude, so radius is much smaller.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.tag: Massive content volume — the key is condensing each topic into process chains.

papers.d: 40 MCQs across cells, molecules, enzymes, membranes, transport, disease. Full A Level weighting shown; AS-only weighting is 31%.
Data-heavy structured items with microscopy math (magnification, actual size = image size/magnification). Full A Level weighting shown; AS-only weighting is 46%.
Laboratory-based Advanced Practical Skills paper; this is not an Alternative to Practical route. Weight shown is for the full A Level.
Energy (respiration & photosynthesis in depth), homeostasis, coordination, inheritance & evolution, biotechnology, ecosystems.
Separate written Planning, Analysis and Evaluation paper; it does not replace Paper 3. Weight shown is for the full A Level.

notes.b: EM structure of organelles; membrane fluid mosaic model; factors affecting diffusion/osmosis; carrier & channel proteins; active transport against gradient.
Protein structure levels (primary→quaternary), denaturation; DNA replication (semi-conservative, Meselson–Stahl); enzymes: Vmax & Km, competitive vs non-competitive inhibition, immobilised enzymes.
Heart cycle & ECG; oxygen dissociation curves (fetal Hb, Bohr shift); xylem & transpiration-cohesion theory; phloem translocation (mass flow); antibodies & vaccination; HIV & immune response.

Respiration: glycolysis → link reaction → Krebs cycle → oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis); photosynthesis: light-dependent (photophosphorylation, photolysis) & Calvin cycle; limiting factors experiments.

Nervous vs hormonal; synapse & drug action; homeostasis (ADH feedback loop); plant hormones (auxins, gibberellins); meiosis & variation; Hardy–Weinberg (p² + 2pq + q² = 1); selection & speciation; genetic engineering & PCR; ecosystems & nutrient cycles.

subjects.fmt: How questions come: data interpretation is king — graphs of enzyme rates, transpiration, oxygen dissociation, population growth; explain questions want mechanism chains ('less ATP produced → less active transport → ...'). P4 essays embedded in structured parts test respiration/photosynthesis detail. P5 requires chi-squared formula & degrees of freedom, and designing fair tests.

flash.a: χ² = Σ((O − E)²/E); degrees of freedom = (rows−1)(columns−1).
p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (p² = homozygous dominant frequency).

flash.q: Where does most ATP form in respiration?
flash.a: Oxidative phosphorylation at the inner mitochondrial membrane (electron transport chain + chemiosmosis).
Active tissues (high CO₂, low pH) shift the oxygen dissociation curve right → Hb releases O₂ more readily.
Light-INDEPENDENT stage of photosynthesis: CO₂ fixed by RuBP (rubisco) → reduced by ATP + NADPH to carbohydrate, in the stroma.

solved.q: In a population, 16% show the recessive phenotype (aa). Find carrier frequency.
Explain why increasing CO₂ beyond a point stops increasing photosynthesis in a greenhouse.
steps: CO₂ is a substrate of the Calvin cycle — initially rate rises with concentration.
Beyond saturation, another factor limits: light intensity (fewer ATP/NADPH) or temperature (enzyme-limited).
Light-dependent stage caps the products the Calvin cycle needs.
solved.a: Law of limiting factors: the factor in shortest supply controls the rate.

practice.q: 1. An image measures 40 mm; magnification ×400. Find actual size.
2. Compare competitive and non-competitive inhibition.
practice.a: Competitive: inhibitor resembles substrate, blocks active site, overcome by more substrate. Non-competitive: binds elsewhere, changes active site shape, NOT overcome by adding substrate.

practice.q: 3. State two roles of ATP in the light-independent stage.
practice.a: Provides energy for the reduction of GP to TP; regenerated from ADP + Pi, also used in regenerating RuBP.

subjects.name: Accounting
subjects.tag: AS = P1 (MCQ) + P2 (Fundamentals, 90 marks); A2 = P3 (75) + P4 (50). Own-figure rule everywhere.

papers.d: 30 MCQs across financial accounting fundamentals.
Answer structured questions: sole traders & partnerships accounts, control accounts, depreciation, adjustments, companies basics, incomplete records, ratios.
Companies in depth (share issues, debentures, revaluations), consolidated basics, cash flow statements, analysis & interpretation, not-for-profit.
Costing: materials/labour/overheads, absorption vs marginal costing, process costing, budgets & variances, investment appraisal (NPV/IRR).

notes.b: Appropriation account: net profit + interest on drawings − salaries − interest on capital = residual shared by PSR. Goodwill on admission/retirement (revaluation method). Current accounts track each partner.
Share capital (ordinary vs preference), share premium account, rights/bonus issues, debentures (loan, fixed interest, NOT shares), dividends (interim vs final), reserves, revaluation surplus.
Operating activities (indirect: profit + depreciation − profit on disposal ± working capital changes), investing, financing; reconcile to cash movement. Learn why profit ≠ cash.
ROCE, asset turnover, gearing (debt/equity), interest cover, EPS, dividend yield, P/E — analyse trend + compare, then advise.

• Absorption vs marginal costing: fixed overheads in product cost vs period cost → profit differences when inventory changes.
  • Process costing with normal/abnormal losses; joint products.
  • Standard costing & variances: material price/usage, labour rate/efficiency, sales price/volume.
  • Investment appraisal: NPV (discount factors), IRR, payback; accept if NPV > 0.

subjects.fmt: How questions come: P2 gives 4 structured questions of 20–25 marks each — prepare full statements in proper format (income statement with 'less: cost of sales' layout, SOFP with standard headings). P3 includes the cash flow statement and interpretation ('advise the bank manager...'). P4 calculations must show formulas: contribution per unit, OAR = overheads ÷ machine hours, NPV table layout.

flash.a: Amount received above nominal value on share issue — goes to a non-distributable share premium reserve.
Credited to the appropriation account (income for the partnership), charged to partners' current accounts.
Absorption includes fixed production overheads in unit cost; marginal treats them as period costs. Profit differs when inventory levels change.
Accept projects with positive NPV (at the company's cost of capital) — they add value.
Debenture = long-term LOAN (fixed interest, creditor); share = part-ownership (dividend only when declared).

solved.q: A & B share 3:2. Net profit $50,000. Interest on capital: A $3,000, B $2,000. B gets salary $6,000. Interest on drawings: A $800, B $500. Divide the profit.
steps: Adjusted profit = 50,000 + 800 + 500 (IoD added back) = 51,300.

solved.q: Machine costs $20,000; annual net cash inflow $8,000 for 3 years; cost of capital 10% (discount factors: yr1 0.909, yr2 0.826, yr3 0.751). Advise.
steps: Negative NPV → reject (or note sensitivity: inflows just $14 short of breakeven).

practice.q: 1. A company issues 10,000 $1 ordinary shares at $1.40. Show the journal entries.
practice.a: Dr Bank 14,000 · Cr Share capital 10,000 · Cr Share premium 4,000.

practice.q: 2. Direct materials cost $12,000; direct labour $8,000; fixed overheads absorbed $5,000 (5,000 units). Find contribution per unit if selling price is $6.
practice.a: Variable cost/unit = (12,000+8,000)/5,000 = $4 → contribution = $2. (Fixed overheads ignored for contribution.)

practice.q: 3. Why is profit not equal to cash flow?
practice.a: Non-cash items (depreciation), timing of credit sales/purchases (working capital), capital expenditure, and financing flows all differ from accrual profit.

subjects.name: Business
subjects.tag: Three papers: P1 (AS concepts), P2 (AS data response), P3 (A2 big case study, 3 hours).

papers.d: Section A: short questions on all 5 AS units. Section B: one structured question (8 & 12 mark parts) — analyse + evaluate with application.
Case-based: 2-, 4-, 6-, 8-mark items; heavy application marks for using case facts and data.
One large pre-released-context case; essays up to 16–20 marks demanding strategy evaluation (Ansoff, Porter, SWOT, PESTLE) and justified recommendations.

notes.b: Entrepreneurship qualities; business planning; organisational design (matrix, flat); leadership styles (autocratic/democratic/laissez-faire/paternalistic); motivation theory applied (Taylor, Mayo, Maslow, Herzberg); recruitment process & training.

Market research methods & sampling; segmentation & targeting; marketing mix deep-dive: product life cycle, Boston matrix, pricing strategies, digital promotion, distribution channels; elasticity basics.
Productivity & efficiency ratios (labour productivity, capacity utilisation); quality management (TQM, quality circles, benchmarking); lean/JIT; network analysis (CPA: critical path, float); R&D.
Cash flow forecasting & improving cash flow; working capital cycle; budgets; final accounts interpretation; business failure causes & remedies.

Ansoff matrix (market penetration → diversification), Porter's 5 forces, generic strategies (cost leadership/differentiation), SWOT & PESTLE, corporate culture, managing change (Kotter), globalisation vs localisation, ethics & stakeholders vs shareholders, contingency planning.

subjects.fmt: How questions come: levels-based marking: K (knowledge) → APPL (application to case) → AN (analysis = because/therefore chains) → EVAL (two-sided, justified verdict). A 12-marker without a conclusion caps around 6. P3 essays: 6-paragraph framework — define terms → argument with case data → counter-argument → both sides weighed → verdict tied to case figures (e.g., 'with $2m cash reserves per Exhibit 3, diversification is affordable').

flash.a: Market penetration, market development, product development, diversification (increasing novelty/risk).
Stars, Cash cows, Question marks (problem children), Dogs — market share vs market growth.
Output per period ÷ number of workers (units/worker or $/worker).
Hygiene factors (salary, conditions — prevent dissatisfaction) vs motivators (achievement, recognition — create satisfaction).
Longest path through the network — determines minimum project duration; activities on it have zero float.

solved.q: 'Evaluate whether opening stores abroad is the best growth strategy for Brand X (home market saturated, strong brand, limited management experience).'
steps: Define market development (Ansoff).
For: saturated home market (case) → new revenue; brand strength transfers; spreading risk.
Against: cultural/market knowledge gaps (limited management experience in case); high set-up cost; political/exchange risks.
Alternatives: product development (leverage brand into new products) — less risky, keeps existing distribution.
Verdict: phased entry (one culturally similar market first) — matches case constraints; pure diversification too risky given management limits.
solved.a: Verdict must cite case constraints — that's the evaluation.

practice.q: 1. Distinguish effectiveness from efficiency with a business example.
practice.a: Effectiveness = doing the right things (achieving objectives, e.g., meeting sales targets). Efficiency = doing things right with least waste (output per input, e.g., units per worker-hour).

practice.q: 2. Calculate capacity utilisation: capacity 10,000 units/month, actual output 7,500.
3. List four elements of a cash flow forecast.
practice.a: Opening balance; cash inflows (receipts) itemised; cash outflows (payments) itemised; closing balance per period.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.tag: P1+P2 (AS) and P3+P4 (A2). The P4 20-mark essay is worth 1/3 of that paper — master the 6-paragraph framework.

papers.d: 30 MCQs on micro + macro AS content.
Section A: data response (20). Section B: micro essay (a 8 + b 12). Section C: macro essay (a 8 + b 12).
30 MCQs: micro + macro + international + development.
Section A: data response (25). Section B: essays — one 20-mark question (1/3 of paper) plus a 10-mark part (b).

notes.b: Demand/supply shifts vs movements; elasticity (PED, PES, YED, XED) with calculations & determinants; consumer/producer surplus; max/min prices; taxation incidence; market failure: externalities (MSC/MPB diagrams), public goods, merit/demerit goods, information gaps; government responses & government failure.

Costs & revenue curves; profit max MR = MC; perfect competition vs monopoly vs monopolistic vs oligopoly (kinked demand); price discrimination; monopsony (minimum wage can raise employment); contestable markets.

GDP/GNP measurement & real vs nominal; AD/AS analysis of growth, inflation, unemployment (types & costs); Phillips curve; balance of payments accounts; exchange rate systems; policies: fiscal, monetary, supply-side (with evaluation: time lags, crowding out, effectiveness conditions).

Comparative advantage & free trade vs protection (tariffs, quotas, subsidies — diagram + infant industry/strategic arguments); trading blocs; terms of trade; Marshall-Lerner & J-curve; balance of payments correction; growth vs development (GDP vs HDI); population & development; role of IMF/World Bank.

subjects.fmt: How questions come: Data response = point + extract data + explanation (never paraphrase the data — quote numbers). 12-mark essays: knowledge → analysis (because/therefore chain) → balanced evaluation with committed conclusion. P4's 20-marker: define all key terms → argument with labelled diagram → counter-argument → weigh (depends on: elasticity, time period, economy's state) → verdict. Diagrams MUST have labelled axes, curves, equilibria and shift arrows.

flash.a: %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP. Determinants: availability of substitutes, necessity vs luxury, proportion of income, time period.
MC = MR; price read off the AR (demand) curve above it.
Non-rivalrous & non-excludable — free-rider problem means markets underprovide them.
Lower unemployment ↔ higher inflation (short run); vertical long run at natural rate (expectations).
Depreciation improves the trade balance only if PED of exports + imports > 1.
GDP = output within the country. GNP = GDP + net income from abroad.

solved.q: Price rises from $4 to $5; quantity falls from 100 to 90 units. Find PED and comment.
steps: PED ≈ 0.47 → inelastic → revenue rises when price rises.

solved.q: 'Assess the view that monopoly is always against the public interest.'
steps: Define monopoly, public interest (price, quality, innovation, equity).
Against monopoly: higher P, lower Q vs perfect competition (diagram: P>MC, welfare loss), X-inefficiency, rent-seeking.
For monopoly situations: economies of scale may mean lower LR prices (natural monopolies like utilities), supernormal profits fund R&D/innovation, contestability disciplines behaviour.
Weigh: depends on barriers' height, regulation (price capping RPI−X), market contestability, dynamic efficiency.
Verdict: regulated monopolies with low contestability harm consumers; but innovative quasi-monopolies (tech) may deliver dynamic gains — judgement with example.
solved.a: Diagram (AR/MR/AC/MC with welfare triangle) + balanced verdict = Level 4.

practice.q: 1. Using AD/AS, explain demand-pull inflation.
practice.a: AD rises (e.g., consumption boom) shifting AD right along near-vertical SRAS → higher price level, small output gain; near full employment the effect is mainly inflationary.

practice.q: 2. Calculate XED: price of good B rises 10%, quantity demanded of good A rises 8%. Relationship?
practice.a: XED = 8/10 = +0.8 → substitutes (positive sign).

practice.q: 3. List four supply-side policies with one drawback each.
practice.a: Education/training (time lag); privatisation (natural monopoly risk); deregulation (safety/environmental risk); tax cuts on profits (may inflate deficit; effect depends on confidence).

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.tag: P1 Approaches + P2 Research Methods (AS); P3 + P4 specialist options (A2). Core studies are the skeleton.

papers.d: Section A: short questions on the 12 core studies. Section B: extended response (essays) on approaches, issues & debates (nature/nurture, reductionism, ethics...).
Scenario-based method questions + a planning question (design a study: aim, hypotheses, variables, sampling, controls, analysis).
Answer from two options (e.g., Abnormal, Health, Sport, Work): key theories & studies.
Applied questions on the same two options + one planning question.

notes.b: Milgram (obedience, 65% to 450V — agentic state, legitimacy of authority); Bandura (Bobo doll — social learning); Andrade (doodling aids concentration); Baron-Cohen (eyes test — theory of mind); Dement & Kleitman (REM & dreams); Hölzel (mindfulness changes brain structure); Piliavin (subway helping — diffusion of responsibility); Saavedra & Silverman (button phobia — single-case method); Fagen (elephant training — operant conditioning); Pozzulo (line-up memory in children); Hassett (monkey toy preferences); Perry (oxytocin & trust).

Experiments (lab/field/natural — control vs ecological validity); observations (participant/covert); self-reports (interviews/questionnaires — social desirability!); case studies; correlations (can't prove causation). Sampling: random, stratified, opportunity, volunteer. Ethics: consent, deception, debrief, withdrawal, protection from harm.

Descriptive: mean/median/mode, range/SD. Inferential: Spearman (correlation), Mann-Whitney (unrelated difference), Wilcoxon (related difference), chi-squared (nominal data). Know when each is used & its interpretation (significance at p ≤ 0.05).

Nature vs nurture; reductionism vs holism; determinism vs free will; individual vs situational; ethics of research; validity types (internal, external, ecological, population); reliability & how to improve (standardisation, inter-rater).

• Abnormal: definitions of abnormality (statistical, deviation from social norms, DSM), schizophrenia & depression explanations/treatments.
  • Health: adherence, pain, practitioner–patient communication.
  • Sport: motivation, arousal, teamwork.
  • Work: groups at work, leadership, satisfaction.
  • And: Child, Cognitive, Law, Environment, Sport & Exercise.

subjects.fmt: How questions come: P1 Section A gives a study scenario and asks 4–6 mark questions ('Outline one result...', 'Give one criticism...'). Section B essays: 'Discuss the contribution of the learning approach...' — describe studies + evaluate. P2 planning question: state IV/DV, write directional/non-directional hypotheses, choose design & justify, sampling method + one weakness, controls, one ethical issue & resolution, how results would be analysed (which test & why).

flash.a: 65% of participants went to the full 450V (all went to at least 300V).
Testing a difference between two UNRELATED groups with at least ordinal data.
Directional (predicts direction of effect) vs non-directional (predicts difference only) — two-tailed is safer unless theory strongly predicts direction.
Two observers record the same behaviour — high agreement = reliable; improved with behaviour checklists/coding systems.
Nomothetic = general laws from many people; idiographic = unique individual understanding (case studies).

solved.q: A researcher compares stress scores (ordinal) of students taught two revision methods (same students do both). Which test and why?
steps: Related groups (same participants both conditions).
Ordinal data, difference sought.
→ Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

solved.q: Give two strengths and two weaknesses of the Bobo doll study.
steps: Strengths: controlled variables → high internal validity; clear operationalised aggression (replicable).
Strength: high inter-rater reliability (observers agreed).
Weakness: artificial doll/clown → low ecological validity (demand characteristics — children 'performing').
Weakness: lab aggression ≠ real-world aggression; cultural/era specificity (1961 USA).

practice.q: 1. Write a directional hypothesis for: effect of caffeine on reaction time.
practice.a: Participants who consume 200mg caffeine will have significantly faster reaction times than those who do not.

practice.q: 2. Why is chi-squared unsuitable for stress scores (interval/ordinal)?
practice.a: Chi-squared needs FREQUENCY counts in NOMINAL categories; ordinal scores violate its data requirements — use Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney instead.

practice.q: 3. Name two ethical issues in Milgram and how each was addressed.
practice.a: Deception (told it was memory study; debriefed, reconciliation letter) · psychological harm (distress — offered right to withdraw, stopped at 450V, debrief).

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.tag: Language analysis at degree-approaching depth: texts, commentary, and language in society.

papers.d: Analysis of unseen non-fiction: comprehension, summary, language/effect questions. Verify timings for your exam year.
Directed writing from stimulus + composition; audience/purpose/register mastery.
Analyse how writers/speakers craft meaning: lexical, grammatical, phonological, discourse features; commentary writing.
Topics: English in the world (global Englishes), child language acquisition; structured questions.

notes.b: Learn to write about: lexis (register, semantic fields, connotation), grammar (syntax, sentence types, modality, pronouns), figurative devices, phonology (alliteration, rhythm, non-fluency features in speech), discourse structure (turn-taking, pragmatics, Grice's maxims).
A-level commentary = select 3–4 significant features, quote precisely, analyse effect, link to audience/purpose/context, and compare across texts. Never feature-spot without meaning.
As 0500 but deeper: controlled argument, rhetorical craft, and precise style commentary on your own writing choices.

Global English: varieties (Singapore, Indian, Nigerian English), codification, ELF. Acquisition: stages of spoken/written development, behaviourist vs innatist (Chomsky LAD) vs interactionist (Bruner) theories, overgeneralisation errors ('goed').

subjects.fmt: How questions come: P3 pairs texts (e.g., a speech and an article on the same theme) and asks for comparative commentary — organise by feature OR by text, but keep comparison live. P4 mixes knowledge questions (theories of acquisition) with applied data analysis (transcript of a child's speech).

flash.a: Quantity (enough info), Quality (truthful), Relation (relevant), Manner (clear). Flouting them creates implicature.
Language Acquisition Device — innate faculty proposing children are born with universal grammar capacity.
Child applies a rule too widely: 'goed', 'mouses' — evidence of rule-learning (supports innatist view).
English as a Lingua Franca — English used between non-native speakers globally; challenges native-speaker norms.

solved.q: Analyse the effect of repetition in a political slogan: 'Yes we can. Yes we did. Yes we will.'
steps: Repetition of modal construction creates rhythm & momentum (phonology).
Tense progression (can → did → will) constructs narrative arc: promise, achievement, future commitment.
Inclusive 'we' builds solidarity — direct appeal to shared identity.
Short declaratives → confident tone; memorable parallelism aids persuasion.
solved.a: Feature → evidence → effect on audience → link to purpose = A-level commentary chain.

practice.q: 1. Distinguish dialect from accent.
practice.a: Accent = pronunciation only; dialect = vocabulary AND grammar features of a variety ('I were' vs 'I was').

practice.q: 2. Give two differences between spoken and written discourse.
practice.a: Spoken: spontaneous, turn-taking, fillers, paralinguistics. Written: planned, edited, permanent, complex subordination.
