subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.tag: Modular 6-unit route: compulsory Pure P1–P4 plus an approved applied pair (S1+S2, M1+M2, S1+M1, S1+D1 or M1+D1). IAS after 3 units; every unit 1h 30m, 75 marks, calculator allowed.

papers.d: Algebra & functions, coordinate geometry, trigonometry, differentiation, integration. Foundation unit — IAS candidates take P1 + P2 + one applied unit.
Proof, sequences & series, exponentials & logarithms, extended trigonometry, further differentiation and integration. Assumes P1.
Advanced algebra & functions, trigonometry, exponentials/logarithms, chain/product/quotient rules, numerical methods. IA2 unit.
Proof by contradiction, binomial expansion, implicit & parametric differentiation, integration by substitution/parts, first-order differential equations, vectors. A* rule: 180/200 UMS across P3+P4.

papers.n: Two of M1, M2, S1, S2, D1
papers.d: Approved pairs only: S1+S2, M1+M2, S1+M1, S1+D1 or M1+D1. M1 = mechanics of particles; S1 = probability & distributions; D1 = algorithms, graphs, linear programming.

notes.b:
• Quadratics: complete the square for vertex form; discriminant b²−4ac decides roots (>0 two, =0 repeated, <0 none).
  • Simultaneous equations: substitution; a line cutting a curve → substitute → quadratic in one variable.
  • Trig: exact values (30/45/60), identities sin²+cos²=1, tan=sin/cos; solve in a given interval — always find ALL solutions.
  • Differentiate then evaluate at a point = gradient of tangent; normal gradient = −1/m.
  • Integrate → +c always; area between curve and x-axis: ∫ y dx between limits; area below axis gives negative value — take modulus.

• Arithmetic: uₙ = a + (n−1)d; sum Sₙ = n/2 (2a + (n−1)d). Geometric: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; sum = a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r); sum to infinity = a/(1−r) for |r|<1.
  • Logs undo powers: aˣ = b ⇔ x = log b / log a. Log laws: log(ab)=log a+log b; log(a/b)=…; log(aⁿ)=n log a.
  • Proof: show / explain steps clearly; counter-example disproves; 'prove' = algebra until LHS = RHS with reasons.
  • Trig equations with identities: replace tan or sin² using identities → quadratic in one trig function.

• Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. Product: v du + u dv. Quotient: (v du − u dv)/v².
  • Stationary points: dy/dx=0 then second derivative >0 min, <0 max (or sign test).
  • Integration by inspection/reverse chain rule: ∫ f′(x)·f(x)ⁿ dx patterns.
  • Numerical methods: iteration xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ); change-of-sign for roots; state that a root lies in interval when f(a), f(b) have opposite signs.
  • Exponential modelling y = Aeᵏᵗ: use two data points to find A and k; doubling/halving time from k = ln2/k.

• Vectors: position vectors, find constants so vectors are parallel (scalar multiple) or perpendicular (dot product = 0).
  • Binomial (1+x)ⁿ for any n: infinite series valid |x|<1; use partial fractions first when denominator factors.
  • Parametric: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); convert to Cartesian by eliminating t.
  • First-order separable DEs: dy/dx = f(x)g(y) → ∫dy/g(y) = ∫f(x)dx then use initial condition to find c.
  • Integration by parts: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du (choose u by LIATE).

• M1 Mechanics: suvat equations for constant acceleration; F=ma; resolve forces at an angle (sin = parallel to slope); moments: force × perpendicular distance.
  • S1 Statistics: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B); E(X)=Σxp, Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]²; Normal distribution standardise Z=(X−μ)/σ.
  • D1 Decision: algorithms (bubble sort, binary search), minimum spanning trees (Kruskal/Prim), shortest path (Dijkstra), critical path analysis, linear programming.
  • Formula booklet is provided — know what is in it so you don't waste time deriving standard results.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: every unit is a 75-mark structured paper — roughly 10–12 questions from about 4 marks to 14 marks, all compulsory, calculators allowed. Early questions are single-skill (differentiate, integrate, solve); later questions chain 3–4 skills (e.g. find k so a line is tangent to a curve). Method marks are generous: always write the formula, substitution, then the answer. Applied units are context-heavy — translate words into models first, then solve.

flash.q: Formula for the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic series?
flash.a: Sₙ = n/2 × (2a + (n−1)d), where a = first term, d = common difference.

flash.q: When does a geometric series have a sum to infinity?
flash.a: Only when |r| < 1; S∞ = a/(1−r).
Differentiate the outer function (leaving inner alone) × derivative of the inner: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

flash.q: Condition for vectors to be perpendicular?
flash.a: Their dot product = 0.

flash.q: What does a change of sign of f(x) between a and b tell you?
flash.a: f has at least one root in the interval (a, b), provided f is continuous.

flash.q: How is the A* in IAL Mathematics decided?
flash.a: Grade A overall (≥480/600 UMS) AND ≥180/200 UMS combined across P3 and P4.

solved.q: Find the equation of the tangent to y = x³ − 2x at the point where x = 2. [4]
steps: dy/dx = 3x² − 2.
At x = 2: gradient = 3(4) − 2 = 10.

solved.q: Solve dy/dx = 2xy, given y = 3 when x = 0. [5]
steps: Separate: dy/y = 2x dx.
Integrate both sides: ln|y| = x² + c.
Exponentiate: y = Ae^(x²) where A = e^c.
Use y=3 at x=0: 3 = Ae⁰ → A = 3.
Standardise: Z = (68 − 60)/5 = 1.6.

practice.q: 1. Find the range of values of k for which x² + 2kx + 5 = 0 has no real roots. [3]
practice.a: Discriminant < 0: (2k)² − 20 < 0 → 4k² < 20 → k² < 5 → −√5 < k < √5.

practice.q: 2. Evaluate ∫₁² (3x² + 1/x) dx, giving your answer in exact form. [4]
practice.a: Antiderivative: x³ + ln|x|. At 2: 8 + ln2; at 1: 1 + 0. Answer = 7 + ln2.

practice.q: 3. A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 14 m/s. Find the maximum height. (g = 9.8 m/s²) [3]
4. Show that the vectors a = (2, 3) and b = (3k, −4) are perpendicular when k = 2. [2]

subjects.name: Further Mathematics
subjects.tag: For students taking Maths + Further Maths. IAS Further = FP1 + two options; full IAL = FP1 + (FP2 or FP3) + two more options from FP2, FP3, M1–M3, S1–S3, D1. All units 1h 30m, 75 marks.

papers.d: Complex numbers, roots of quadratic equations, numerical methods, parabola & rectangular hyperbola coordinate systems, matrix algebra, transformations, series (method of differences), proof by induction. Compulsory for both IAS and IAL Further Maths.
Inequalities, further series, De Moivre's theorem, first- and second-order differential equations, Maclaurin & Taylor series, polar coordinates. IA2 option — one of FP2/FP3 required.
Hyperbolic functions, further coordinate systems (ellipse, hyperbola), reduction formulae, arc length, triple scalar product, planes, eigenvalues & eigenvectors. IA2 alternative to FP2.

papers.n: Two more from M1–M3, S1–S3, D1
papers.d: Any two units beyond FP1 and the FP2/FP3 choice — Mechanics 1–3, Statistics 1–3 or Decision 1. Units already used for IAL Mathematics cannot be reused for Further Maths.

notes.b:
• Complex arithmetic: add component-wise; multiply and use i² = −1; conjugate z̄ flips the sign of the imaginary part.
  • Quadratics with negative discriminant: roots come in conjugate pairs a ± bi; sum = −b/a, product = c/a still hold.
  • Argand diagrams: modulus |z| = √(x²+y²), argument = angle from positive real axis (−π < θ ≤ π).
  • Proof by induction template: base case → assume n = k → prove n = k+1 using the assumption → conclusion 'true for all n ≥ …'.
  • Method of differences: split terms (e.g. 1/r − 1/(r+1)) so middle terms cancel, leaving first and last.

• 2×2 matrices multiply row × column; determinant = ad − bc; inverse = (1/det) × swapped-diagonal, sign-flipped matrix.
  • Det = 0 → singular → no inverse; a singular matrix maps the plane to a line through the origin.
  • Standard matrices: rotation θ → [[cosθ, −sinθ],[sinθ, cosθ]]; reflection in x-axis → [[1,0],[0,−1]].
  • Composite transformation: multiply matrices RIGHT to LEFT (the matrix nearest the column vector acts first).
  • Invariant points satisfy M·x = x — solve (M − I)x = 0.

• De Moivre: (cosθ + i sinθ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ; expand with binomial to get multiple-angle formulae.
  • zⁿ = 1 has n roots equally spaced around the unit circle (angles 2πk/n).
  • Second-order linear DEs: solve auxiliary equation → complementary function; add a particular integral matching the RHS form (try Ae²ˣ for e²ˣ, etc.).
  • Maclaurin: f(x) = f(0) + f′(0)x + f″(0)x²/2! + …; standard results for eˣ, sin x, cos x, ln(1+x), (1+x)ⁿ.
  • Polar curves: convert with x = r cosθ, y = r sinθ; area = ½∫ r² dθ.

• Hyperbolics: cosh x = (eˣ+e⁻ˣ)/2, sinh x = (eˣ−e⁻ˣ)/2; cosh² − sinh² = 1.
  • d/dx cosh x = sinh x; d/dx sinh x = cosh x — but arcsinh/arccosh involve 1/√(x²±1).
  • Eigenvalues: solve det(M − λI) = 0; eigenvector from (M − λI)v = 0; diagonalisation M = PDP⁻¹.
  • Reduction formula: integrate by parts to relate Iₙ to Iₙ₋₂ or Iₙ₋₁, then iterate down to a base case.
  • Triple scalar product a·(b×c) = volume of parallelepiped; plane: r·n = p.

• Taking Maths + Further Maths uses 12 units total — each unit can only count towards ONE qualification.
  • Engineering route: M1–M3 stack builds mechanics depth beyond the single M1/M2 allowed in Maths.
  • Statistics route: S1–S3 for data science / actuarial paths.
  • A* in Further Maths: grade A overall (≥480/600) AND ≥270/300 across your best three IA2 units.
  • Plan the staging across series: FP1 + two AS options early, FP2/FP3 in the final series.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: FP papers are dense and proof-heavy — expect 'show that', induction, and multi-step algebra carrying 8–12 marks. Complex numbers, matrices and DE questions reward clean structure: define, method, working, statement. Options share the style of the main Maths applied units but at greater depth (M3 circular motion, S3 chi-squared and regression).

flash.q: What are the roots of z² + 4 = 0?
If z = 3 + 4i, what is |z| and the argument?
flash.a: |z| = 5; arg z = arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.927 rad.
When its determinant ad − bc = 0.
(cosθ + i sinθ)ⁿ = cos(nθ) + i sin(nθ).
1 (hyperbolic identity).

flash.q: How is the A* in IAL Further Mathematics decided?
flash.a: Grade A overall (≥480/600 UMS) AND ≥270/300 across the best three IA2 units.

solved.q: Given that z = 2 + i is a root of z³ − 6z² + az + b = 0, find the real constants a and b. [5]
steps: Roots of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs → z = 2 − i is also a root.
Sum of all three roots = 6 → third root = 6 − (2+i) − (2−i) = 2.
Product of roots = −b (for z³ + pz² + qz + r: product = −r). Roots: (2+i)(2−i)(2) = 5 × 2 = 10 → b = −10.
Sum of products in pairs = a: (2+i)(2−i) + 2(2+i) + 2(2−i) = 5 + 4 = 9 → a = 9 (sign per expansion: coefficient of z is a).

solved.q: Solve d²y/dx² − 5dy/dx + 6y = 0. [4]
steps: Auxiliary equation: m² − 5m + 6 = 0 → (m−2)(m−3) = 0 → m = 2, 3.
Distinct real roots → complementary function y = Ae²ˣ + Be³ˣ.
RHS = 0 so no particular integral needed.

solved.q: Prove by induction that [[1,2],[0,1]]ⁿ = [[1,2n],[0,1]] for all positive integers n. [5]
steps: Base n=1: LHS = the matrix itself, RHS = [[1,2],[0,1]] ✓.
Assume true for n=k: Mᵏ = [[1,2k],[0,1]].
True for n=1 and n=k ⇒ n=k+1, so true for all n ≥ 1.
solved.a: Proven: Mⁿ = [[1,2n],[0,1]] for all positive integers n.

practice.q: 1. Find the inverse of the matrix [[4, 3],[2, 2]]. [2]
2. Use the method of differences to find Σ 1/(r(r+1)) from r = 1 to n. [4]
practice.a: 1/(r(r+1)) = 1/r − 1/(r+1); terms cancel leaving 1 − 1/(n+1) = n/(n+1).

practice.q: 3. Find the eigenvalues of [[3, 1],[2, 4]]. [3]
4. Differentiate y = arccosh(2x). [2]

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.tag: Six-unit modular science with two dedicated practical-skills papers (Units 3 & 6). IAS = Units 1–3; full IAL = all six. Units 1–3: 1h 30m theory, 1h 20m practical; Units 4–5: 1h 45m.

papers.d: Mechanics, materials. Mix of multiple-choice, short open, open-response, calculations and extended writing; ≥32 marks target Level-2+ maths skills.
Waves & particle nature of light, electric circuits. Same question-type mix as Unit 1.
Written paper testing the techniques from Units 1–2: experiments, data handling, graphs, uncertainty.
Momentum, circular motion, SHM, gravitational & electric fields, capacitors, particle physics. May include synoptic content.
Thermal physics, nuclear radiation, oscillations, astrophysics & cosmology.
Written paper testing the techniques from Units 4–5, including planning and evaluation.

notes.b:
• suvat only for CONSTANT acceleration; draw a velocity–time graph when acceleration changes.
  • Newton's 2nd: F = ma (vector form for 2D). Weight = mg.
  • Moments: force × perpendicular distance from pivot; equilibrium → Σmoments clockwise = Σanticlockwise AND ΣF = 0.
  • Work = F × d (force along motion); KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh; power = work ÷ time.
  • Materials: Hooke F = kx; stress = F/A; strain = Δx/x; Young modulus = stress/strain; energy stored = ½Fx = area under force–extension graph.

• Wave equation v = fλ; refraction from n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂; critical angle sin C = 1/n (to air).
  • Interference: path difference = nλ constructive, (n+½)λ destructive; Young's double slit w = λD/s.
  • Photoelectric equation: hf = φ + KEmax — one photon ejects one electron; threshold frequency f₀ = φ/h.
  • Circuits: V = IR; series adds R, parallel adds 1/R; power P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
  • EMF = terminal p.d. + lost volts: ε = V + Ir; internal resistance from gradient of V–I graph.

• Momentum conserved in ALL collisions: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
  • Circular motion: a = v²/r = ω²r toward centre; F = mv²/r.
  • SHM: a = −ω²x; T = 2π/ω; vmax = ωA; energy swaps between KE and PE.
  • Gravity: F = Gm₁m₂/r²; g = GM/r²; field strength radial.
  • Electric fields: F = kQq/r², E = V/d uniform; capacitors: Q = CV, E = ½QV = ½CV².

• Ideal gas: pV = nRT; Boltzmann pV = NkT; internal energy = sum of molecular KE + PE.
  • Specific heat: Q = mcΔθ; specific latent heat Q = mL during phase change (no Δθ).
  • Nuclear: A = Z + N; α = ⁴₂He nucleus, β⁻ = fast electron, γ = EM wave; activity A = λN; half-life T½ = ln2/λ.
  • Oscillations: free vs forced vs damped (light/heavy/critical); resonance when driving frequency ≈ natural frequency.
  • Cosmology: redshift z = Δλ/λ; Hubble v = Hd; Big Bang evidence: CMBR and redshift.

• Independent variable = what YOU change; dependent = what you measure; control everything else.
  • Uncertainty: resolution of instrument for single readings; (max−min)/2 or half-range for repeats.
  • Graphs: label axes with quantity/unit; gradient and intercept carry the marks — rearrange to y = mx + c form first.
  • Percentage uncertainty = uncertainty/value × 100; combine by adding percentages.
  • Evaluation: accuracy (closeness to true value) vs precision (repeatability); random errors scatter, systematic errors shift.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: multi-step structured questions, usually 4–8 marks each, with the mark scheme split into 'state' (1), 'explain' (2–3 linked points), and 'calculate with working' (3–5, where formula → substitution → answer with unit earns the marks). Definition questions demand exact phrasing. Practical units give unfamiliar experiments — marks come from describing fair tests, plotting, gradient work and evaluating uncertainty, so practise writing methods in numbered steps.

flash.a: Resultant force = rate of change of momentum (F = ma for constant mass).
hf = φ + KEmax — photon energy = work function + max kinetic energy of ejected electron.
Driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system.

flash.q: Relationship between half-life and decay constant?
flash.a: T½ = ln2/λ.

flash.q: What does the gradient of a V–I graph for a battery give?
flash.a: Negative internal resistance; the y-intercept is the EMF.

flash.q: Formula for fringe spacing in Young's double slit?
flash.a: w = λD/s (wavelength × slit-to-screen distance ÷ slit separation).

solved.q: A battery of EMF 12 V delivers a current of 2.0 A with terminal p.d. 11 V. Find the internal resistance. [3]
steps: Lost volts = ε − V = 12 − 11 = 1 V.

solved.q: Light of frequency 7.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz shines on a metal with work function 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) [3]
steps: Photon energy E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 7.0 × 10¹⁴ = 4.64 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
(≈ 1.4 eV if divided by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.)

solved.q: A 0.20 kg ball on a 1.5 m string moves in a horizontal circle at 3.0 m/s. Find the tension in the string. [3]
steps: Centripetal force F = mv²/r = 0.20 × 9/1.5.
Tension provides the centripetal force (horizontal component).

practice.q: 1. A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s over 120 m. Find its acceleration. [3]
2. Define specific latent heat of fusion. [2]
practice.a: Energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point, with no temperature change.

practice.q: 3. Calculate the wavelength of a 200 Hz sound wave in air (v = 340 m/s). [2]
4. Explain why the activity of a radioactive sample decreases over time. [2]
practice.a: The number of undecayed nuclei N falls; activity A = λN, so it decreases exponentially, halving every half-life.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.tag: Six units: IAS = Units 1–3, full IAL adds Units 4–6. Two dedicated written practical papers (Units 3 & 6, 1h 20m, 50 marks). Theory units 1–2: 1h 30m/80; units 4–5: 1h 45m/90.

papers.n: Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry
papers.d: Atomic structure, bonding, shapes, intermolecular forces and first organic chemistry. Section A objective questions + structured/extended items; Periodic Table provided.
Energetics, redox, Group 2 & 7 chemistry, halogenoalkanes, alcohols.
Written paper on the practical techniques from Units 1–2: titrations, calorimetry, rates, qualitative tests.
Kinetics, equilibrium (Kc), acid–base, further organic mechanisms; may include synoptic content.
Transition metal chemistry, electrode potentials, further organic nitrogen compounds, analysis.
Written paper on advanced practical analysis and evaluation from Units 4–5.

notes.b:
• Ionic: giant lattice, conducts when molten/aqueous, high m.p. Covalent: simple molecular (low m.p.) vs giant covalent (diamond, SiO₂ — very hard, high m.p.).
  • Shapes by electron pairs (VSEPR): 2 linear 180°, 3 trigonal planar 120°, 4 tetrahedral 109.5°, 6 octahedral 90°; lone pairs compress angles (NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°).
  • Intermolecular forces: van der Waals < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding (needs N–H, O–H or F–H).
  • Organic basics: alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (substitution with Cl₂/UV), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (addition, decolourise bromine water), isomerism.
  • Atom economy = (mass desired product ÷ mass all products) × 100 — the green-chemistry metric.

• ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants); exothermic ΔH < 0. Calorimetry: q = mcΔθ; divide by moles for ΔH per mole.
  • Hess cycles: ΔH(reaction) = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants); bond enthalpies give approximate ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made.
  • Group 2: reactivity ↑ down (easier to lose 2e⁻); solubility of hydroxides ↑ down, sulfates ↓ down.
  • Group 7: oxidising power ↓ down (F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂); halogen displacement: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.
  • Halogenoalkanes: nucleophilic substitution (OH⁻), elimination with ethanolic KOH; rate depends on C–X bond strength (C–I fastest).

• Rate = gradient of concentration–time graph (tangent for curve); orders from initial-rates table: doubling [A] doubles rate → first order.
  • Rate equation: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ; k has units depending on overall order.
  • Arrhenius idea: higher T → more molecules exceed activation energy → k increases.
  • Kc = [products]ᵖ/[reactants]ʳ at equilibrium; only temperature changes Kc; catalyst speeds BOTH directions equally — no shift.
  • Le Chatelier: increase pressure → side with fewer gas moles; increase concentration → system consumes the added species.

• pH = −log[H⁺]; Ka for weak acids; titration curves: strong acid–strong base equivalence pH = 7, weak acid–strong base > 7.
  • OIL RIG; half-equations balanced for atoms then charge, electrons added to the more positive side.
  • Electrode potentials: more positive E° = stronger oxidising agent; cell EMF = E°(cathode) − E°(anode).
  • Transition metals: variable oxidation states (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu⁺/Cu²⁺), coloured ions (d-orbital splitting), catalytic activity; [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ blue, with excess NH₃ deep blue solution.
  • Chromate/dichromate redox titrations: dichromate in acid is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green).

• Amines: basic (lone pair on N accepts H⁺); primary amines from reduction of nitriles (LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni).
  • Amides: from acyl chloride + amine; hydrolyse in acid/base.
  • Carbonyl chemistry: nucleophilic addition of HCN to aldehydes/ketones; 2,4-DNPH = orange precipitate identifies C=O.
  • Tests: Tollens' (aldehyde → silver mirror), Fehling's (aldehyde → brick-red), iodoform (CH₃CO– group → yellow ppt).
  • Analysis: IR (C=O ~1700 cm⁻¹, O–H broad 2500–3300), mass spec (molecular ion = Mᵣ; fragmentation), nmr environments.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: Section A objective items then structured questions building from recall to multi-step application. 'Explain' questions need linked statements (particle behaviour → property). Calculations (calorimetry, Kc, titrations, electrode potentials) carry method marks — always write the formula, substitution and answer with units. Organic questions reward mechanisms with curly arrows and correct partial charges. Practical units describe an unfamiliar experiment and ask you to plan, process data and evaluate.

flash.q: Shape and bond angle of methane vs water?
flash.a: CH₄ tetrahedral 109.5°; H₂O bent 104.5° (two lone pairs compress the angle).

flash.q: What is the trend in oxidising power down Group 7?
flash.a: Decreases: F₂ strongest, I₂ weakest — displacement happens only when the added halogen is more reactive.

flash.q: What does a catalyst do to Kc?
flash.a: Nothing — it speeds attainment of equilibrium but does not shift the position or change Kc.

flash.q: Cell EMF from standard electrode potentials?
flash.a: E°cell = E°(more positive electrode, reduction) − E°(other electrode).

flash.q: Which test distinguishes aldehydes from ketones?
flash.a: Tollens' reagent: aldehydes give a silver mirror; ketones do not react.
(Mᵣ of desired product ÷ Σ Mᵣ of all products) × 100%.

solved.q: 0.020 mol of acid neutralised raises 100 g of solution temperature by 5.0 °C. Find ΔH per mole. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹) [3]
steps: q = mcΔθ = 100 × 4.18 × 5.0 = 2090 J released.
Exothermic → ΔH = −105 kJ/mol (3 s.f.).

solved.q: For A ⇌ 2B, 1.0 mol A in 1.0 dm³ reaches equilibrium with 0.60 mol of B. Find Kc. [4]
steps: Change: B formed 0.60 mol → A used = 0.60/2 = 0.30 mol.
Equilibrium moles: A = 1.0 − 0.30 = 0.70; B = 0.60.
V = 1.0 dm³ so [A] = 0.70, [B] = 0.60 mol/dm³.
Kc = [B]²/[A] = 0.36/0.70 = 0.51 mol dm⁻³ (units depend on the equation).

solved.q: Write the half-equation for the reduction of dichromate(VI) to chromium(III) in acid. [2]
steps: Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺: balance Cr, then O with H₂O (7 H₂O right), then H with H⁺ (14 H⁺ left).
Balance charge with electrons: left charge = −2 +14 = +12; right = +6 → add 6e⁻ left.

practice.q: 1. Explain why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium. [3]
practice.a: Both metallic; Mg²⁺ has greater charge and smaller ionic radius than Na⁺ → stronger attraction to the electron sea → more energy needed to separate the ions.

practice.q: 2. A reaction is first order in A and second order in B. State the rate equation and overall order. [2]
practice.a: rate = k[A][B]²; overall order 3.

practice.q: 3. Calculate the pH of 0.050 mol/dm³ HCl. [2]
4. Name the product and conditions: ethene + steam. [2]
practice.a: Ethanol, via addition with a phosphoric acid catalyst at ~300 °C and high pressure.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.tag: Six units: IAS = Units 1–3; full IAL = all six. Practical skills tested in written Units 3 & 6 (1h 20m, 50 marks). Theory units 1–2: 1h 30m/80; units 4–5: 1h 45m/90.

papers.d: Biological molecules, digestion, diet, the circulatory system, heart disease. MCQ, calculations, structured and extended writing.
Cell structure and microscopy, cell division, development, biodiversity, conservation, plant structures.
Written paper on the 18 core-practical techniques from Units 1–2: variables, reliability, graphing.
Photosynthesis, respiration, energy transfer, ecosystems, microbiology, immunity; may include synoptic content.

papers.n: Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination & Gene Technology
papers.d: Respiration detail, homeostasis, nervous and hormonal coordination, gene technology.
Written paper on advanced practical skills from Units 4–5: planning investigations, statistical tests (incl. t-test), data presentation.

notes.b:
• Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose) → disaccharides (maltose, sucrose) → polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) by condensation; broken by hydrolysis.
  • Tests: Benedict's (reducing sugar → brick-red), iodine (starch → blue-black), biuret (protein → purple), ethanol emulsion (lipid → cloudy).
  • Proteins: primary sequence → secondary (α-helix, β-pleated) → tertiary (3D, bonds incl. disulfide bridges) → quaternary (multi-subunit, e.g. haemoglobin).
  • Enzymes: lock-and-key/induced fit; denatured by high temperature or extreme pH; rate limited by substrate concentration then enzyme concentration.
  • Heart disease risk factors: saturated fat, salt, smoking, inactivity; HDL 'good' vs LDL 'bad' cholesterol.

• Resolution = smallest distance two points remain distinguishable: electron microscopes beat light microscopes by ~100×.
  • Mitosis: one division → 2 identical diploid cells (growth/repair); meiosis: two divisions → 4 genetically different haploid cells (gametes).
  • Stem cells: totipotent → pluripotent → differentiated; ethical debates around embryo use.
  • Biodiversity measured by species richness + evenness; Simpson's index combines both (higher = more diverse).
  • Conservation: in situ (reserves, national parks) vs ex situ (zoos, seed banks).

• Photosynthesis: light-dependent stage (thylakoid, ATP + NADPH, photolysis of water → O₂); Calvin cycle (stroma, fixes CO₂ into GP → GALP → glucose).
  • Respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → link reaction + Krebs (mitochondrial matrix) → oxidative phosphorylation (cristae); 38 ATP max from glucose (aerobic).
  • Ecology: 10% energy transfer between trophic levels (respiration, heat, waste); pyramids of energy always upright.
  • Immunity: phagocytosis (ingest + lyse pathogens), lymphocytes (B → plasma cells making antibodies; T → kill infected cells directly + helper role).
  • Vaccination = artificial active immunity: antigen triggers memory cells without disease.

• Homeostasis: negative feedback loops (receptor → control centre → effector); blood glucose — insulin lowers (glycogenesis), glucagon raises (glycogenolysis).
  • Nervous vs hormonal: fast+short vs slow+long; reflex arcs bypass the brain for speed.
  • Synapse: neurotransmitter diffuses across cleft, binds receptors, new impulse in post-synaptic neurone.
  • Gene technology: restriction enzymes cut, ligase joins, vectors (plasmids) carry; PCR amplifies DNA in vitro; gel electrophoresis separates by size (smaller fragments travel further).
  • Genetic engineering applications: insulin production, GM crops, gene therapy (adding/correcting genes).

• Valid = answers the question; reliable = repeatable (replicates); precise = narrow spread / fine scale.
  • Independent/dependent/control variables define a fair test.
  • Draw graphs: ruled axes, sensible scale, points + line of best fit; describe the pattern with data quotes.
  • Statistics: t-test compares two means (needs p < 0.05 to reject the null); chi-squared for frequencies; correlation for association (not causation).
  • Evaluation questions: link EACH limitation to a specific improvement — not vague answers.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: structured multi-part questions mixing recall, data interpretation and extended writing (6–9 mark 'suggest an explanation' items). Marks go to precise biological vocabulary: say 'water potential gradient', not 'water concentration'; 'active site denatured', not 'enzyme died'. Practical papers give unfamiliar contexts from the 18 core practicals — practise describing methods in numbered steps and interpreting statistical test outcomes.

flash.q: Products of photolysis in the light-dependent stage?
flash.a: Oxygen, hydrogen (to NADPH) and ATP.

flash.q: Where does the Krebs cycle occur?
flash.a: Mitochondrial matrix.
Mitosis: 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis: 4 genetically different haploid cells for gametes.

flash.q: Benedict's test result for a reducing sugar?
flash.a: Brick-red precipitate on heating.
Immunity from a vaccine: antigens trigger antibody production and memory cells without causing the disease.
Only ~10% of energy transfers to the next trophic level; the rest is lost in respiration, heat and waste.

solved.q: A heart beats 72 times per minute with a stroke volume of 70 cm³. Calculate cardiac output. [2]
steps: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
= 72 × 70 = 5040 cm³/min ≈ 5.0 dm³/min.

solved.q: A leaf fixes 0.12 g of CO₂ per hour. Given a light intensity increase doubles the rate, find the new mass fixed in 3 hours. [3]
steps: Original rate: 0.12 g/h. New rate: 0.24 g/h.

solved.q: In peas, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). Two heterozygous plants are crossed. Find the expected phenotypic ratio. [3]
steps: Cross Tt × Tt → gametes T, t each.
Offspring: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
Phenotypes: 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

practice.q: 1. Explain why enzymes stop working at high temperature. [3]
practice.a: Heat breaks the bonds holding the tertiary structure; the active site loses its shape (denatures), so the substrate no longer fits — reaction rate falls to zero.

practice.q: 2. Describe how a t-test is used in biology. [3]
practice.a: Compares the means of two data sets to test whether a difference is significant: calculate t, compare with the critical value at p = 0.05; if t exceeds the critical value, reject the null hypothesis.

practice.q: 3. State two differences between arteries and veins. [2]
practice.a: Arteries: thick muscular walls, carry blood away from heart under high pressure, no valves. Veins: thinner walls, valves present, carry blood to heart.

practice.q: 4. What does gel electrophoresis separate and how? [2]
practice.a: DNA fragments by size: samples in wells migrate through a gel when a current is applied; smaller fragments travel further toward the positive electrode.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.tag: Four equal units, each 25% of the IAL. IAS = Units 1–2; full IAL = all four. Units 1–2: 1h 45m; Units 3–4: 2h. Every paper mixes MCQs, short answers, data response and essays.

papers.d: Section A: 6 MCQs (6). Section B: 5 short-answer (20). Section C: five-part data-response from a source booklet (34). Section D: one 20-mark essay from a choice of two.
Same structure as Unit 1 — inflation, unemployment, growth, balance of payments, macro policy.
Section A: 6 MCQs (6). Section B: five-part data response (34). Section C: two 20-mark essays from a choice of three. Assumes Units 1–2.
Same structure as Unit 3 — globalisation, trade, exchange rates, development economics. Assumes Units 1–3.

notes.b:
• Demand curve slopes down (income/substitution effects); supply slopes up; equilibrium where they cross.
  • Shifters: demand — income, prices of substitutes/complements, tastes, population; supply — costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of firms.
  • Elasticities: PED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP (price elastic if >1 — luxuries with substitutes); PES depends on spare capacity and time.
  • Incidence: with inelastic demand, consumers bear most of a tax; subsidy benefits the inelastic side more.
  • Consumer surplus = below demand curve, above price; producer surplus = above supply, below price. Both lost as deadweight loss under mis-set intervention.

• Perfect competition: many firms, homogeneous product, P = MC = AC minimum in long run, zero economic profit.
  • Monopoly: one firm, price maker, barriers to entry; profit max at MC = MR; deadweight loss vs competition.
  • Oligopoly: few interdependent firms — game theory (prisoner's dilemma), kinked demand, collusion risk.
  • Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, excess capacity in long run.
  • Efficiency: allocative (P = MC), productive (min AC), dynamic (innovation over time).

• GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); real GDP strips inflation; per capita divides by population; growth % = Δreal GDP/GDP × 100.
  • Inflation: CPI vs RPI; causes — demand-pull, cost-push, monetary, imported.
  • Unemployment: claimant vs ILO; causes — cyclical, structural, frictional, seasonal.
  • Balance of payments: current account (trade in goods/services, income, transfers) + capital/financial accounts.
  • Trade-off: Phillips curve links low unemployment with higher inflation short-run.

• Fiscal: government spending + taxation (G, T) — expansionary in recessions; automatic stabilisers (progressive tax, benefits).
  • Monetary: interest rates (cost of borrowing, exchange rate channel) and quantitative easing.
  • Supply-side: education, infrastructure, deregulation — shifts LRAS right, non-inflationary growth.
  • Exchange rates: floating vs fixed; appreciation helps importers, hurts exporters (PED decides).
  • Global: comparative advantage (opportunity cost), tariffs/quotas effects, WTO, development indicators (HDI), poverty traps.

• 20-mark essay = KAA (knowledge, application, analysis ~12) + evaluation (~8). Two-sided judgement required.
  • Structure: define key terms → diagram → chain of reasoning (because… therefore…) → real-world example → counter-argument → justified conclusion.
  • Diagrams must be labelled: axes (P, Q), curves (D, S, MC, MR, AD, AS), shifts shown with arrows and new equilibrium marked.
  • Evaluation phrases: 'however, this depends on…', 'in the long run…', 'the magnitude matters because…'.
  • Keep a file of current examples (central bank rate decisions, oil shocks, trade disputes) to apply in data-response and essays.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: Unit 1–2 papers: 6 MCQs, then 5 short answers (4 marks each — define + one applied point), a five-part data response (extract then calculate/explain/evaluate), and one 20-mark essay from a choice of two. Units 3–4 replace the short answers with a second essay choice. MCQs test definitions and small chains; data responses quote the booklet; essays reward two-sided argument with diagrams. Calculators are allowed and quantitative skills (~10–15%) appear throughout.

flash.q: Formula for price elasticity of demand?
flash.a: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price (ignore the sign).

flash.q: Where does a profit-maximising firm produce?
flash.a: Where MC = MR (marginal cost = marginal revenue).
GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).

flash.q: Name two causes of cost-push inflation.
flash.a: Rising input costs (oil/wages) and supply shocks — e.g. OPEC cuts or a depreciating currency raising import prices.
Producing where opportunity cost is lowest; trade lets both countries gain even if one is absolutely better at everything.

flash.q: What does an appreciation of the currency do to exports?
flash.a: Makes them more expensive abroad → export demand falls (magnitude depends on PED).

solved.q: A firm cuts price from $10 to $9 and quantity sold rises from 100 to 115. Calculate PED and interpret. [3]
steps: PED = 13.95/10.5 ≈ 1.33 > 1 → demand is price elastic; revenue rises.
solved.a: PED ≈ 1.33 (elastic) — the price cut increases total revenue.

solved.q: A monopolist has MC = 10 and faces P = 50 − 2Q (so TR = 50Q − 2Q²). Find the profit-maximising output and price. [4]
steps: MR = dTR/dQ = 50 − 4Q.

solved.q: CPI rises from 120 to 126 in a year. Calculate the inflation rate. [2]
steps: ΔCPI = 6.

practice.q: 1. Using a diagram, explain the effect of a subsidy on consumers. [4]
practice.a: Subsidy shifts supply right (S→S₁): price falls P→P₁, quantity rises; consumer incidence = share of the subsidy passed on as lower prices — larger when demand is price inelastic.

practice.q: 2. Distinguish between structural and cyclical unemployment. [4]
practice.a: Structural: long-term mismatch of skills/location (declining industries), needs retraining. Cyclical: caused by deficient aggregate demand in recessions, falls when demand recovers.

practice.q: 3. Evaluate ONE supply-side policy. [6]
practice.a: E.g. education spending: raises labour productivity → LRAS shifts right → non-inflationary growth and lower natural unemployment. Evaluation: long time-lag, fiscal cost, depends on quality/employability of courses.

practice.q: 4. A currency depreciates 10%. Explain two effects on the economy. [4]
practice.a: Exports cheaper abroad → export demand rises (AD up, growth) but imports dearer → imported inflation; effect sizes depend on PED and import content of consumption.

subjects.name: Business
subjects.tag: Four units of equal 25% weight. IAS = Units 1–2; full IAL = all four. Every unit: 2 hours, 80 marks, source-based with a 20-mark essay. Exams in January, June and October.

papers.d: Section A: short/extended-response on sources (30). Section B: source-based (30). Section C: one 20-mark essay on source material.
Finance, resource management and external influences — same section structure as Unit 1.
Section A: source-based questions (40). Sections B & C: 20-mark essays each, synoptic across Units 1–2.
Section A: source-based (40). Sections B & C: 20-mark essays, synoptic across Units 1–3, often on a pre-released context.

notes.b:
• Marketing mix (7P): product, price, place, promotion + people, process, physical evidence.
  • Segmentation: demographic, geographic, psychographic, behavioural → target market → positioning.
  • Pricing: cost-plus, penetration (low entry), skimming (high then drop), price discrimination, competitive.
  • Product lifecycle: introduction → growth → maturity → decline; extension strategies (new uses, new markets, redesign).
  • Branding: adds perceived value, customer loyalty, price premium — but costly to build and maintain.

• Cash flow ≠ profit: profit includes accruals; businesses fail on cash timing, not profit figures. Forecast cash flow, chase receivables, hold buffer stock of cash.
  • Working capital = current assets − current liabilities; too low risks insolvency, too high wastes returns.
  • Ratio toolkit: gross margin = GP/Revenue; ROCE = operating profit/capital employed × 100; current ratio; gearing = debt/(debt+equity).
  • Capacity utilisation = actual/max × 100; lean production (JIT, kaizen) cuts waste but needs reliable suppliers.
  • Break-even: output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit; margin of safety = expected − break-even output.

• Ansoff matrix: market penetration (lowest risk) → product development / market development → diversification (highest risk).
  • Porter's Five Forces: rivalry, new entrants (barriers), substitutes, buyer power, supplier power — strong forces squeeze profits.
  • SWOT internal (strengths, weaknesses) vs PESTLE external (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental).
  • Investment appraisal: payback (years to recover), ARR (% return), NPV (discounts future cash flows — best method).
  • Change management: Kaizen continuous vs big-bang; Kotter's 8 steps; resistance from staff — communicate and involve.

• Motives to expand abroad: saturated home market, economies of scale, resource access, risk spread.
  • Entry modes: exporting < licensing < franchising < joint venture < FDI (wholly owned subsidiary) — control rises with commitment and risk.
  • Globalisation drivers: trade liberalisation (WTO), technology, transport, MNC networks.
  • Exchange-rate exposure: appreciation hurts export competitiveness; hedging with forwards/options.
  • Ethics & sustainability: labour standards, environmental footprint, tax avoidance — stakeholder vs shareholder view.

• Point → because (chain of reasoning) → evidence from the case → so what (link back to the question).
  • Balance: one counter-argument with a response, then a justified conclusion anchored in the case data.
  • Quantitative questions: state the formula, calculate, then INTERPRET for the business (not just the number).
  • Command words: 'analyse' needs chains; 'evaluate' needs two sides + judgement; 'assess' needs judgement with reasons.
  • Use the source booklet: quote figures and facts — application marks reward case-specific answers.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: source-based papers. Units 1–2: two 30-mark source sections plus a 20-mark essay; Units 3–4: a 40-mark source section plus two 20-mark essays (choose from two in B, compulsory in C — check the paper each series). Quantitative skills are embedded: ratios, break-even, investment appraisal — always show working. Essays demand chains of reasoning and a justified conclusion that references the case; pre-learned answers without application score poorly.

flash.a: Fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit (price − variable cost per unit).
Producing/receiving components only as needed — cuts inventory costs but leaves no buffer against supply shocks.

flash.q: Name the four Ansoff growth strategies.
flash.a: Market penetration, market development, product development, diversification.
Return on capital employed = operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100% — efficiency of capital use.

flash.q: Which investment appraisal method accounts for the time value of money?
flash.a: NPV (net present value) — future cash flows are discounted back to today's value.

flash.q: Order of global market entry modes by increasing commitment?
flash.a: Exporting → licensing → franchising → joint venture → wholly owned subsidiary (FDI).

solved.q: A firm sells at $25 per unit, variable cost $15, fixed costs $40 000. Find break-even output and margin of safety if it sells 5 000 units. [4]
steps: Contribution per unit = 25 − 15 = $10.
Break-even = 40 000 ÷ 10 = 4 000 units.
Margin of safety = 5 000 − 4 000 = 1 000 units (20% of sales).
solved.a: Break-even 4 000 units; margin of safety 1 000 units.

solved.q: A project costs $50 000 today and returns $30 000 in year 1 and $30 000 in year 2. With a 10% discount rate, find the NPV. [4]
steps: Total PV = 52 066.

solved.q: A retailer buys at $12 and sells at $20. Find the gross profit margin. [2]
steps: GP per unit = 20 − 12 = $8.

practice.q: 1. Analyse two benefits of market segmentation. [6]
practice.a: Focused marketing spend on the most profitable groups (higher conversion); tailored products/pricing match needs better → loyalty and price premium. Both raise revenue relative to undifferentiated marketing.

practice.q: 2. A firm's current ratio is 0.8. Explain two possible problems and one remedy. [5]
practice.a: Problems: may struggle to pay short-term debts (liquidity risk); suppliers may demand cash-on-delivery, straining cash further. Remedy: raise long-term finance, sell idle assets or renegotiate creditor terms.

practice.q: 3. Using Porter's Five Forces, explain why airline profits are often low. [6]
practice.a: High rivalry (many comparable rivals, perishable seats); strong buyer power (price comparison sites); substitutes (rail, video meetings); suppliers (aircraft makers, fuel) concentrated and powerful. Only low entry barriers regionally prevent worse.

practice.q: 4. Evaluate franchising as an entry mode into a new country. [8]
practice.a: Fast low-capital expansion with local knowledge and motivated owner-managers (royalty income). However: loss of control over quality, brand risk from one bad franchisee, profit shared — strongest when brand standards are enforceable.

subjects.name: Accounting
subjects.tag: Four equal units. IAS = Units 1–2 (1h 45m each); IA2 = Units 3–4 (2h each). Every unit: 80 marks, 25% of the IAL, structured questions on practical scenarios.

papers.d: Double entry, books of prime entry, control accounts, bank reconciliation, depreciation, break-even and basic costing. Structured scenario questions.
Final accounts of sole traders, partnerships and limited companies; incomplete records; ratios and interpretation; concepts and ethics.
Absorption and marginal costing, budgets and variance analysis, investment appraisal, limiting-factor decisions.
Published company accounts, IAS 7 cash-flow statements, accounting standards, capital structure and full ratio analysis.

notes.b:
• Every transaction: debit one account, credit another — DEBITS = assets + expenses; CREDITS = capital + liabilities + revenue (remember DEAD CLIC).
  • Books of prime entry: sales/purchases day books, returns books, cash book, journal — then posted to ledgers.
  • Trial balance: check debits = credits — it catches one-sided errors but NOT errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry or reversal.
  • Control accounts: sales ledger control = total receivables; purchases ledger control = total payables; reconcile to the ledgers.
  • Bank reconciliation: update cash book (standing orders, direct debits, bank charges, dishonoured cheques), then reconcile timing items (unpresented cheques, uncredited deposits).

• Straight line: (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life. Reducing balance: net book value × fixed %.
  • Disposals: compare proceeds with NBV → profit/loss on disposal in the income statement.
  • Adjustments: accruals (owed, add to expense), prepayments (paid ahead, deduct), bad debts (write off), provision for doubtful debts (% of receivables).
  • Income statement → gross profit → operating profit → profit for the year; SOFP at year-end with non-current assets, working capital, less non-current liabilities.
  • Partnerships: appropriation account — salaries, interest on capital/capital, residual shared by PSR; current accounts track drawings.

• Cost classification: fixed vs variable; direct vs indirect (overheads need allocation → apportionment → absorption).
  • Absorption costing spreads overheads into units; marginal costing writes them off in the period — profit differs when inventory changes.
  • Break-even = FC ÷ contribution per unit; contribution = price − variable cost; C/S ratio for multi-product.
  • Budgets: master budget = production → purchases → labour → cash. Flex the budget to actual volumes before comparing variances.
  • Variances: materials (price + usage), labour (rate + efficiency); adverse = actual worse than standard — investigate material ones.

• Payback: cumulative cash flow hits zero — ignores time value and later flows.
  • ARR = average annual profit ÷ initial investment × 100 — uses profit not cash, ignores timing.
  • NPV: discount each year's net cash flow at the cost of capital; accept if NPV > 0. Discount factors given: PV = amount × DF.
  • Limiting factors: rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce resource (kg, hours), produce in that order up to demand.
  • Make-or-buy: compare supplier price with marginal (relevant) cost of making — ignore absorbed overheads that continue either way.

• Limited companies: share capital (ordinary/preference), share premium account, reserves; dividends appropriated from retained earnings, NOT an expense.
  • IAS 7 cash flow (indirect): operating (profit + depreciation ± working capital), investing (non-current asset purchases/sales), financing (share issues, loans, dividends paid).
  • Ratios: profitability (ROCE, margins), liquidity (current, acid test), efficiency (inventory/receivables/payables days), gearing (debt ÷ capital employed), investor (EPS, dividend cover, P/E).
  • Interpretation: ALWAYS compare — year on year, budget vs actual, and industry norms; a number alone earns little credit.
  • Creative accounting red flags: aggressive revenue recognition, capitalising costs, changing depreciation policy — window-dressing the accounts.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: structured scenario questions (a full set of books for one fictional business) where each part builds on earlier figures — so check each number as you go. Presentation marks: proper headings ('Income statement for the year ended…'), correct line-item names, workings referenced (W1, W2). Theory questions reward definitions with an example. Interpretation questions demand judgement: ratios → trend/benchmark → cause → consequence for the business.

flash.q: What does DEAD CLIC stand for?
flash.a: Debits: Expenses, Assets, Drawings. Credits: Liabilities, Income, Capital.
(Cost − residual value) ÷ useful life in years.
Years until cumulative net cash flow ≥ 0 (use the last negative year + remainder/next year's flow).
Selling price − variable cost per unit.
(Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities.

flash.q: Where do dividends appear in company accounts?
flash.a: They are an appropriation of retained earnings (movement in equity), never an expense in the income statement.

solved.q: A sales ledger control account shows $48 200 but the list of customer balances totals $47 300. Identify two reconciling items that explain the difference. [4]
steps: Possible timing differences: a cash receipt posted to the control account but not yet to a customer's account in the sales ledger (or vice versa).
Errors: the sales journal total posted incorrectly, a credit note omitted from one side, or a set-off (contra) with the purchases ledger recorded on only one side.
Each item adjusts ONE side only — hence control vs ledger differ.
solved.a: Examples: unposted cash receipt; omitted credit note or contra entry (any two valid).

solved.q: A firm makes 10 000 units, sells 9 000. Fixed overheads $50 000, variable cost $4/unit, price $10. Find the profit difference between absorption (overheads absorbed on all production) and marginal costing. [4]
steps: Fixed overhead per unit (absorption) = 50 000/10 000 = $5.
Inventory = 1 000 units → inventory carries 1 000 × 5 = $5 000 of fixed cost on the balance sheet under absorption.
Marginal costing expenses all $50 000 this period → absorption profit is $5 000 HIGHER when inventory rises.
solved.a: Absorption profit exceeds marginal profit by $5 000 (inventory increase × fixed overhead per unit).

solved.q: Machine costs $18 000; cash inflows $8 000 (yr1), $9 000 (yr2), $9 000 (yr3). Cost of capital 10% (DFs: 0.909, 0.826, 0.751). Find payback and NPV. [6]
steps: Cumulative: yr1 8 000; yr2 17 000; yr3 26 000 → payback in yr 3: 1 + 1 000/9 000 = 2.11 years.

practice.q: 1. A trial balance fails to agree. List four types of error NOT revealed by it. [4]
practice.a: Errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, compensating errors and complete reversal of entries.

practice.q: 2. Closing inventory is $12 400 (unit price $8). Using FIFO, what is the inventory quantity and how does rising input cost affect reported profit under FIFO? [4]
practice.a: 12 400 ÷ 8 = 1 550 units. Under FIFO the oldest (cheaper) costs hit cost of sales, so when input prices rise FIFO reports higher profit than weighted average.

practice.q: 3. Calculate the receivables collection period: credit sales $720 000, trade receivables $60 000. [2]
practice.a: Receivables days = 60 000/720 000 × 365 = 30.4 ≈ 30 days.

practice.q: 4. Explain why a high gearing ratio worries a lender. [4]
practice.a: High debt relative to equity means large fixed interest obligations ahead of shareholders; in a downturn profit may not cover interest (high financial risk), so the lender may demand security or refuse credit.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.tag: Four units. IAS = Units 1–2 (1h 45m, 50 marks each); IA2 = Units 3–4 (2h, 50 marks each). All papers analyse unseen texts from a source booklet.

papers.d: Section A: context and identity. Section B: the creation of voice. Two compulsory questions analysing unseen texts from the Source Booklet.
Section A: spoken language today. Section B: written language of the 19th–21st century — how English varies and changes globally.
Section A: creating text. Section B: commentary on your own writing choices — both sections compulsory.
Section A: unseen data analysis. Section B: extended response — both on the SAME topic, chosen from the paper's options.

notes.b:
• Lexis: word choice, semantic fields, connotation, register, jargon, dialect/archaism/coinage.
  • Grammar & syntax: word classes, sentence types (declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamative), coordination vs subordination, active vs passive, ellipsis.
  • Phonology: rhyme, rhythm, alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia; in speech — stress, intonation, pace.
  • Pragmatics: implicature (meaning beyond words), politeness strategies, face (Brown & Levinson), speech acts.
  • Discourse & graphology: turn-taking, topic management, cohesion (anaphora, conjunctions); layout, typography, images, emojis.

notes.t: 2. Language levels in speech vs writing
notes.b:
• Speech: spontaneous, planned-in-real-time → fillers, false starts, hedging, contractions, deixis (context-dependent: 'this', 'here'), tag questions, overlapping turns.
  • Writing: permanent, planned → complete sentences, standard punctuation, embedded clauses, careful lexis; but electronic messaging blends features (emojis, abbreviations, ellipsis with conversational tone).
  • Mode continuum: a formal letter ≠ a WhatsApp voice note — classify by dominant features, not label alone.
  • Context = audience, purpose, mode, genre, and the relationship between participants (power/solidarity).
  • Idiolect (personal) vs sociolect (group) — identity is constructed through choices at every level.

• Change mechanisms: borrowing (from other languages), neologism/coinage, compounding, blending, acronymy, clipping, affixation, semantic shift (broadening/narrowing, pejoration/amelioration).
  • Causes: technology, social change, contact with other languages, fashion, youth culture.
  • Attitudes: prescriptivists defend 'correctness'; descriptivists document actual usage — evaluate both positions with evidence.
  • World Englishes: Kachru's circles (inner/outer/expanding); pidgins and creoles as contact languages.
  • Child language: imitation vs innateness (Skinner vs Chomsky), caregiver speech ('motherese'), stages of acquisition.

• Section A (creating text): write in an unfamiliar form/genre for a specified audience and purpose — match register, structure and rhetorical devices to the task.
  • Section B (commentary): analyse your own choices using the framework terms — name the feature, quote it, explain its effect for audience/purpose.
  • Commentary formula: 'I used X (feature) in order to Y (effect), which suits the audience because Z.'
  • Plan with a quick audience/purpose/mode grid before writing; drafts earn nothing — write once, carefully.
  • Rhetorical toolkit for persuasive writing: triads, anaphora, direct address ('you'), hyperbole, emotive imagery, rhetorical questions, statistics, expert opinion.

• Section A: apply frameworks to fresh unseen data — structure answers: identify → quote → analyse effect → link to context.
  • Section B: extended response on ONE topic — build an argument with evidence: topic sentence, framework analysis, example, link back.
  • Key topics include language and gender, language and power, language and technology, language change, child language development.
  • Deploy theorists precisely: Fairclough (power/synthetic personalisation), Lakoff (deficit vs dominance), Tannen (difference), Crystal (change attitudes), Kachru (World Englishes) — name + claim + application.
  • Comparison habit (Units 1–2): integrate — 'whereas Text A…, Text B…' — never analyse one text fully then the other.

subjects.fmt: How the questions come: every unit is built on UNSEEN texts in a source booklet — you cannot pre-learn answers, only methods. Analytical questions follow: identify a feature, quote precisely, analyse its effect, connect to audience/purpose. The 25-mark items (Units 1–2) reward integrated comparison across two texts plus conceptualised comment (context/identity/change). Unit 3 rewards controlled, audience-aware writing plus a precise commentary; Unit 4 rewards a well-evidenced argument about a topic. Timing: 1.75 min per mark.

flash.q: Name the six framework areas of language analysis.
flash.a: Lexis, grammar, phonology, pragmatics, discourse, graphology.

flash.q: Give four features of spontaneous speech.
flash.a: Fillers, false starts, contractions, tag questions, ellipsis, overlap, deixis — any four.
Fairclough's term for addressing a mass audience as if speaking to an individual ('you') — common in advertising.

flash.q: Define semantic narrowing with an example.
flash.a: A word's meaning becomes more specific over time — e.g. 'meat' once meant any food, now only flesh.

flash.q: What are the three Kachru circles of English?
flash.a: Inner (native: UK, USA), outer (second language: India, Nigeria), expanding (foreign language: China, Egypt).
Feature + quote + intended effect + link to audience/purpose: 'I used X in order to Y, suiting this audience because Z.'

solved.q: Text A is a formal complaint letter; Text B is a tweet about the same issue. Outline a four-point comparative answer about voice and context. [8]
steps: Opening point: both share purpose (complaint) but mode/register diverge — formal written vs electronic brevity.
Text A: full sentences, standard punctuation, modal verbs ('I would appreciate') convey politeness-as-power-distance; passive voice ('the item was delivered') keeps focus on the issue.
Text B: contractions, ellipsis, hashtag as graphological cohesion and community address; direct emotion lexis signals solidarity with followers.
Synthesis: the same speech act (complaint) is reshaped by audience relationship — institutional vs peer — showing identity constructed through register choices.
solved.a: Any four well-linked comparative points quoting both texts earn the marks — integrate, don't sequence.

solved.q: From a transcript of a radio interview, identify three features showing the interviewee is constructing an expert identity. [6]
steps: Lexical: technical terms/jargon in their field ('longitudinal data') excluding outsiders.
Pragmatic: confident assertions, minimal hedging; managing the agenda by extending answers beyond the question.
Discourse: taking longer turns, using the interviewer's first name (synthetic solidarity), reformulating questions to favour their angle.
solved.a: Three named features each tied to identity construction with quotes — 2 marks each.

solved.q: 'Text messaging is destroying the English language.' Discuss with reference to change mechanisms. [10]
steps: Position: texting accelerates existing mechanisms — clipping ('uni'), initialisms/acronyms ('lol'), blending, emoji as paralinguistic graphology.
Evidence: historical parallels — printing, telegraph, telephony all spawned moral panic (Crystal: each medium adapts language, doesn't destroy it).
Counter: concerns about formal writing standards in schoolwork; register awareness is the real skill.
Judgement: language is being extended, not destroyed — users code-switch by context.
solved.a: Mechanisms named + historical evidence + evaluated counter = top band.

practice.q: 1. Identify the mode, audience and purpose of a gym's Instagram story, giving three supporting features. [6]
practice.a: Mode: electronic/multimodal. Audience: young followers → informal register. Purpose: promote + engage. Features: imperatives ('Swipe up!'), emojis as graphology, hashtags for discourse community — each tied to audience/purpose.

practice.q: 2. Explain the difference between a pidgin and a creole. [4]
practice.a: Pidgin: simplified contact language with no native speakers, limited vocabulary/grammar. Creole: a pidgin that has become a community's first language, expanding vocabulary and grammar (e.g. Jamaican Creole).

practice.q: 3. What is 'motherese' (caregiver speech) and why does it matter? [4]
practice.a: Simplified, exaggerated, high-pitched speech to infants: short sentences, repetition, concrete referents. It tunes phonemic awareness and models turn-taking — evidence for social interaction in acquisition.

practice.q: 4. Plan the commentary for a persuasive article you wrote: name four features you would explain and their effects. [8]
practice.a: Any four: triad for memorability; direct address 'you' to create involvement; statistics with source for credibility (logos); emotive anecdote for pathos — each quoted and linked to the target reader.
